Chapter 4

The Experimental Setup

4.1 The Large Hadron Collider

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) [74] is the world’s most powerful particle accelerator,

located at CERN near Geneva, Switzerland. It is designed to collide proton and heavy ion

beams at unprecedented energies to explore fundamental aspects of particle physics. The

LHC is a circular accelerator with a circumference of 27 kilometers, approximately 100

meters underground. It operates in four collision modes: (a) proton–proton (pp) collisions,

which is the primary mode for exploring the Standard Model and searching for new physics;

(b) proton–Lead (p–Pb) collisions, which provide insight into the behavior of partons in

nuclear matter; (c) Lead–Lead (Pb–Pb) collisions, essential for studying the quark-gluon

plasma and the properties of strongly interacting matter at extreme energy densities; and

(d) Xenon–Xenon (Xe–Xe) collisions, used to probe intermediate-sized nuclei and study

system-size effects in heavy-ion physics. The LHC hosts four main experiments, each

with a specific physics focus. ATLAS and CMS are general-purpose detectors optimized

for high-precision measurements in pp collisions, including Higgs boson studies, searches

for supersymmetry, and beyond-Standard Model phenomena. ALICE is dedicated to the

study of strongly interacting matter in heavy-ion collisions, particularly the quark-gluon

plasma. LHCb focuses on the physics of b-hadrons, enabling precise studies of CP violation

and rare decays in the flavor sector. Together, these experiments form a comprehensive



40

program that explores a wide range of fundamental questions in high-energy physics.

For the purpose of this thesis, moving forward, I will only discuss the pp collisions.

Between 2016-2018, called Run-2 of the LHC, the protons were collided at 13 TeV.

To achieve proton–proton (pp) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the

LHC utilizes a sophisticated chain of accelerators that gradually increase the energy of

protons before they enter the main collider ring. The process begins with a hydrogen gas

source, where protons are extracted via electric fields. These protons are first accelerated

by LINAC2 (replaced by LINAC4 for Run 3 and beyond) to an energy of approximately 50

MeV. From there, the beam is injected into the Proton Synchrotron Booster, which raises

the energy to around 1.4 GeV. The beam is then transferred to the Proton Synchrotron

(PS), where it is accelerated further to 25 GeV. The final stage of the pre-acceleration chain

is the Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS), which boosts the protons to 450 GeV before they

are ready for injection into the LHC. A schematic overview is shown in Figure 4.1.

Once in the LHC, the protons circulate in two separate beam pipes housed within a

single tunnel, traveling in opposite directions. These beams are further accelerated to their

final energy of 6.5 TeV per beam, culminating in a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy at the

interaction points. Acceleration within the LHC ring is achieved through a series of radio-

frequency (RF) cavities, which provide precise electric fields to increase the kinetic energy

of the particles during each turn around the ring. The proton beams are grouped into

tightly packed bunches, with thousands of bunches circulating in the machine, separated

by nanoseconds. These bunches are timed to collide at the designated interaction points

where the detectors, including CMS, are located.

Maintaining stable and well-defined trajectories for the high-energy beams requires the

use of advanced superconducting magnets, which are among the most critical components

of the LHC. The primary magnets are dipole magnets, of which there are over 1232 in the

LHC. These magnets generate a magnetic field of 8.33 Tesla to bend the proton beams

along the circular path of the accelerator. In addition to dipoles, the LHC employs 392

quadrupole magnets for beam focusing. These function similarly to lenses in optics, alter-

between collisions and are ready to record fresh data from each subsequent bunch crossing.

frev is the revolution frequency, γr is the relativistic Lorentz factor, εn is the normalized

transverse emittance, β∗ is the value of the beta function at the interaction point (IP),

and F is the geometric luminosity reduction factor accounting for the crossing angle at

the IP. Increasing Nb and nb leads to higher particle densities and more frequent collisions,

while minimizing εn and β∗ improves the transverse overlap of the colliding beams. The

value of β∗ is particularly critical: reducing it results in a smaller beam size at the IP,

thus enhancing the collision probability. However, such reductions impose stringent re-

quirements on the optics and stability of the beam. The geometric factor F , typically less

than one, accounts for the fact that beams do not collide head-on but at a small crossing

angle to avoid parasitic interactions elsewhere in the ring. Optimizing these parameters

is a central task in maximizing LHC performance.

At high instantaneous luminosities, a single bunch crossing can result in multiple in-

elastic proton–proton interactions, a phenomenon known as pileup. These additional in-

teractions overlay the hard-scattering event of interest and pose a significant challenge

for event reconstruction. Pileup can be classified as either in-time, originating from in-

teractions within the same bunch crossing, or out-of-time, resulting from energy deposits



44

left by interactions in neighboring bunch crossings due to the finite response time of the

detector subsystems. During Run 2 of the LHC, the average number of interactions per

bunch crossing often exceeded 30, and occasionally surpassed 50 during periods of peak

luminosity. This high pileup environment complicates the reconstruction of physics ob-

jects. Sophisticated pileup mitigation techniques, including charged-hadron subtraction

and pileup per particle identification (PUPPI), are employed to minimize its impact and

preserve the precision of physics measurements.

4.2 The CMS experiment

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) [77, 78] is a general-purpose detector located at one

of the four primary interaction points along the LHC ring. It is designed to explore a

broad range of physics at the TeV scale, from precision measurements of SM processes

to searches for physics beyond the SM, including the production of dark matter. The

detector recorded pp collision data at a centre-of-mass energy of
√
s = 13 TeV during the

Run-2 data-taking period from 2016 to 2018, accumulating a total integrated luminosity

of approximately 138 fb−1, which forms the dataset used in this analysis.

Despite its substantial mass—approximately 14,000 tonnes, this detector is referred

to as compact because it achieves its functionality within a comparatively small radial

footprint relative to its capabilities. This compactness is made possible by the use of

a high-field, 3.8 T superconducting solenoid magnet, which enables precise momentum

measurements in a limited volume. The solenoid itself is 13 m long and 6 m in diameter.

This strong magnetic field causes charged particles to curve as they traverse the detector,

allowing their momenta to be measured from the curvature of their reconstructed tracks.

The solenoid defines the overall architecture of the detector: the tracking and calorimetry

systems are housed inside the solenoid volume, while the muon detectors are embedded in

the steel flux-return yoke that surrounds it. This design choice to place the full calorimetry

inside the coil distinguishes CMS from ATLAS and allows for a more compact but higher-

field configuration.



45

The detector is designed with a layered, cylindrical geometry that provides nearly

hermetic coverage of the solid angle around the interaction point. Moving radially out-

ward from the beam axis, the detector consists of the silicon pixel and strip tracker, the

lead tungstate crystal electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL), the brass-scintillator hadronic

calorimeter (HCAL), the superconducting solenoid, and the muon system interleaved with

the steel return yoke. Each barrel region is complemented by endcap detectors on either

side, extending the pseudorapidity coverage to |η| < 5 for calorimeter measurements and

|η| < 2.4 for tracking and muon reconstruction. The hermetic design is essential for the

reliable reconstruction of missing transverse momentum pmiss
T , which is the primary experi-

4.4 Silicon tracker

The CMS tracker [79] is the innermost detector subsystem, surrounding the interaction

point and designed to provide precise measurements of the trajectories of charged parti-

cles produced in pp collisions. It is fully constructed from silicon-based detector technolo-

gies and operates within the 3.8 T axial magnetic field provided by the superconducting

solenoid, which causes charged particles to follow helical paths whose curvature is used to

determine their momenta. The tracker covers a pseudorapidity range of |η| < 2.4 and is

designed to reconstruct tracks with high efficiency and low fake rate in the high-occupancy

environment of the LHC, where multiple pp interactions occur within each bunch crossing.

The tracker is divided into two main components: the pixel detector and the strip de-

tector. The pixel detector occupies the innermost region, closest to the interaction point,

and consists of four barrel layers (BPIX) and three endcap disks on each side (FPIX), pro-

viding three-dimensional hit measurements with a spatial resolution of approximately 10

µm in the transverse plane. This high granularity is essential for the precise reconstruction

of primary and secondary vertices, which is critical for identifying jets originating from

b-quark hadronization, which is a central requirement of the mono-Higgs(bb̄) analysis. The

pixel detector was upgraded during the LHC Run-2 period to improve its performance at

high instantaneous luminosity, with the four-layer configuration providing robust tracking

even in the presence of significant pileup.



48

Surrounding the pixel detector is the silicon strip tracker, which extends radially from

approximately 20 cm to 110 cm and is organized into the Tracker Inner Barrel (TIB),

Tracker Outer Barrel (TOB), Tracker Inner Disks (TID), and Tracker EndCaps (TEC).

The strip detector provides additional track measurements that improve the momentum

resolution and extend the lever arm for track reconstruction. The combination of pixel

and strip hits allows tracks to be reconstructed with a transverse momentum resolution

of δpT/pT ≈ 1− 2% for typical charged particles relevant to this analysis.

The tracking information plays a central role in several aspects of the mono-Higgs

analysis. Precise vertex reconstruction allows the identification of the primary interaction

vertex among the many pileup vertices present in each event, which is essential for the

correct assignment of jets and for the computation of the missing transverse momentum.

Furthermore, the impact parameter and secondary vertex information provided by the

tracker are the key inputs to the b-tagging algorithms used to identify the H → bb̄ decay.

4.5 Electromagnetic calorimeter

The electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) [80] is a hermetic, homogeneous calorimeter

constructed from lead tungstate (PbWO4) scintillating crystals, and is designed to measure

the energy of electrons and photons with high precision [81]. Lead tungstate was chosen

for its short radiation length (X0=0.89 cm) and small Moliere radius (2.2 cm), which

allow the construction of a compact calorimeter with fine transverse granularity. The

scintillation light produced in the crystals is detected by avalanche photodiodes (APDs)

in the barrel and vacuum phototriodes (VPTs) in the endcaps, chosen for their ability to

operate in the high magnetic field environment.

The ECAL is divided into a barrel region (EB) covering |η| < 1.479 and two endcap

regions (EE) covering 1.479 < |η| < 3.0. The barrel consists of approximately 61,200

crystals arranged in a quasi-projective geometry, each with a cross-section of approxi-

mately 22×22 mm2 corresponding to ∆η ×∆ϕ ≈ 0.0174× 0.0174. A preshower detector

(ES), consisting of two planes of silicon strip sensors interleaved with lead absorbers, is



49

placed in front of the endcap crystals to improve the spatial resolution and assist in the

discrimination between photons and π0 → γγ decays.

4.6 Hadronic calorimeter

The hadronic calorimeter (HCAL) [83] is designed to measure the energy of hadrons and

hadronic jets, and together with the ECAL forms the calorimetric system used for jet

energy measurements and pmiss
T reconstruction. The HCAL is a sampling calorimeter,

using brass as the absorber material and plastic scintillator tiles as the active medium, with

the scintillation light read out via wavelength-shifting fibers and hybrid photodetectors.

Brass was chosen for its short nuclear interaction length combined with its non-magnetic



50

properties, which is important given the location of much of the HCAL inside the solenoid.

The HCAL is organized into four distinct subsystems. The Hadron Barrel (HB) cov-

ers |η| < 1.4 and is located between the ECAL and the solenoid coil, with a depth of

approximately 5.8 nuclear interaction lengths at η = 0, increasing toward higher |η|. To

compensate for the limited depth available inside the solenoid, the Hadron Outer (HO)

detector is placed outside the solenoid in the barrel region, using the solenoid material

as an additional absorber to catch late-starting showers and improve the measurement

of energetic jets. The Hadron Endcap (HE) extends the coverage to |η| < 3.0, while

the Hadron Forward (HF) calorimeter, based on steel absorbers and quartz fibers with

Cherenkov light readout, extends the hermetic coverage to η| < 5.2. This forward cover-

age is crucial for reducing the rate of fake pmiss
T arising from mismeasured jets at high |η|,

which is particularly important for a search relying on large pmiss
T as the primary signature.

The energy resolution of the HCAL for single pions is approximately σE/E ∼ 100%/

particle-flow framework, which improves the effective jet energy resolution by using the su-

perior tracking and ECAL measurements for the charged and electromagnetic components

of the jet, and reserving the HCAL primarily for the neutral hadronic component. The

HCAL energy scale and resolution are calibrated using dijet, γ+jet, and Z+jets events.

In the context of the mono-Higgs(bb̄) analysis, the HCAL plays a central role in jet

energy measurements and pmiss
T reconstruction. The accurate measurement of hadronic

recoil, including the Higgs candidate jet in the merged category and the pair of b-tagged

jets in the resolved category, depends critically on the HCAL response and its calibration.

Mismeasured jet energies in the HCAL are one of the primary sources of instrumental

fake pmiss
T , and dedicated noise filters and jet quality criteria are applied to suppress such

contributions, as described in the analysis section.

4.7 Muon system

The CMS muon system is the outermost detector subsystem, located outside the supercon-

ducting solenoid and embedded in the steel flux-return yoke. Muons are the only charged

particles that penetrate the calorimeters with minimal energy loss, making the muon sys-

tem the primary detector for their identification and momentum measurement. The muon

system serves a dual purpose: it provides standalone muon reconstruction using hits in the

muon detectors alone, and it improves the overall muon momentum measurement when

combined with the inner tracker in a global fit. The system covers a pseudorapidity range

of |η| < 2.4 and uses three complementary gaseous detector technologies.

In the barrel region (|η| < 1.2), where the muon rate and background occupancy

are relatively low and the residual magnetic field in the return yoke is small, drift tube

(DT) chambers are used. The DT system consists of four stations of chambers interleaved

with the iron yoke layers, providing measurements of the muon position and direction

with a spatial resolution of approximately 100µm per chamber. In the endcap regions

(0.9 < |η| < 2.4), where the muon flux and neutron-induced background are higher and

the magnetic field in the yoke is less uniform, cathode strip chambers (CSCs) are used

instead. CSCs are multi-wire proportional chambers with cathode strip readout, offering

a spatial resolution of approximately 75–150 µm and the ability to operate at high rates.

Resistive plate chambers (RPCs) are deployed in both the barrel and endcap regions,

covering |η| < 1.9, and provide fast timing signals with a time resolution of approximately

1 ns, which is used primarily for bunch crossing identification and triggering.

The muon momentum is measured using a global fit that combines the track recon-

structed in the silicon tracker with the hits in the muon stations. For muons with pT < 200

GeV, the tracker dominates the momentum resolution, and the combined muon momen-

tum resolution is approximately 1–2% in the barrel. At higher momenta, the muon system

hits become increasingly important for constraining the track curvature. The muon iden-

tification efficiency is typically above 95–98% for isolated muons in the kinematic range

relevant to this analysis, with a misidentification rate for hadrons that punch through the



52

calorimeters of well below 1%.

In the mono-Higgs(bb̄) analysis, the muon system is essential for the definition of the

lepton control regions used to constrain the dominant backgrounds.

4.8 Trigger system

The LHC delivers pp collisions at a bunch crossing rate of 40 MHz, corresponding to an

interaction rate far exceeding what can be read out and stored for offline analysis. The

CMS trigger system [84] is responsible for reducing this rate by several orders of magnitude

while retaining the physics processes of interest with high efficiency. It is organized into

two sequential stages: the Level-1 (L1) trigger [85], implemented in custom hardware,

and the High-Level Trigger (HLT) [86], implemented in a farm of commercial processors

running a streamlined version of the CMS reconstruction software.

The L1 trigger operates with a fixed latency of 3.2 µs and reduces the bunch crossing

rate from 40 MHz to a maximum output rate of approximately 100 kHz. It uses coarse-

granularity information from the calorimeters and muon detectors, the tracker is not read

out at L1 due to latency constraints, to identify candidate physics objects such as electrons,

photons, muons, jets, and pmiss
T . The L1 decision is made using programmable logic in

field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and is based on the presence, multiplicity, and

transverse energy of these candidate objects above configurable thresholds. During Run-2,

the L1 trigger underwent a significant upgrade, introducing time-multiplexed processing

that allows the full calorimeter information to be processed in a single processor at each

bunch crossing, substantially improving the energy resolution and object identification

capability at L1.

Events accepted by the L1 trigger are passed to the HLT, which further reduces the

rate to approximately 1 kHz for permanent storage. The HLT has access to the full

detector readout and runs a simplified but complete version of the offline reconstruction

algorithms, including tracking, calorimeter clustering, and particle-flow reconstruction,

within a processing time budget of approximately 300 ms per event. The HLT is organized

Chapter 5

Simulation and Reconstruction

5.1 Event simulation

Accurate simulation of proton–proton collision events is essential for interpreting the data

collected by the CMS detector and for enabling meaningful comparisons between experi-

mental results and theoretical predictions. Event simulation underpins nearly every aspect

of collider physics analyses: it is used to optimize event selection strategies, estimate back-

ground contributions, derive detector efficiencies and resolution corrections, and quantify

systematic uncertainties. By modeling both the underlying particle interactions and the

CMS detector response, simulation allows the experimental measurements to be related

back to fundamental parameters in theoretical models.

The generation of simulated events begins with the modeling of the hard scattering

process at parton level. Matrix element generators such asMadGraph5 aMC@NLO [87]

are employed to compute scattering amplitudes at leading order (LO) or next-to-leading

order (NLO) in perturbative QCD, depending on the precision required. These generators

provide flexible tools for simulating a wide range of SM and BSM processes with varying

final-state multiplicities. The resulting partonic events are then interfaced with parton

shower generators such as PYTHIA8 [88], which simulate the subsequent evolution of

the system through initial-state and final-state radiation, parton showering, hadroniza-

tion, and the underlying event. This yields a list of stable or long-lived particles that



56

approximate the observable final state in the detector.

Following the generation of the final-state particles, full detector simulation is per-

formed to model the response of the CMS detector. This step is carried out using

GEANT4 [89], a toolkit that simulates the passage of particles through matter based on

detailed physical processes, including electromagnetic and hadronic interactions, energy

loss mechanisms, multiple scattering, and nuclear effects. The CMS detector geometry,

material composition, and readout characteristics are encoded within this framework, al-

lowing a realistic emulation of how particles would interact with each subdetector. This

results in digitized output signals that emulate those produced by the actual CMS data

acquisition system.

These digitized signals are then processed through the standard CMS reconstruction

chain, which includes clustering, tracking, calorimeter energy deposits, and high-level ob-

ject identification such as electrons, muons, and jets. To reproduce realistic experimental

conditions, additional inelastic pp interactions are overlaid on the simulated events to

emulate pileup, matched to the distribution observed in data. Although computationally

demanding, full simulation provides the highest-fidelity model of CMS data. In scenarios

requiring high-statistics samples where full simulation would be prohibitively resource-

intensive, CMS also employs fast simulation techniques. These use parametrized detector

responses and simplified geometries while preserving essential physics characteristics, of-

fering a trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency.

5.2 Object reconstruction

The reconstruction of high-level physics objects from raw detector information is a critical

step in converting recorded or simulated CMS events into meaningful data for analysis.

These objects — such as electrons, muons, jets, and missing transverse momentum —

are used to apply event selections, compute physical observables, and define signal and

control regions. The performance of object reconstruction directly impacts the sensitivity

of searches and precision measurements, making it essential that the reconstruction algo-



57

rithms are optimized for efficiency, resolution, and robustness under varying detector and

pileup conditions.

At CMS, object reconstruction is based on a sophisticated approach known as the

Particle Flow (PF) algorithm [82]. PF combines information from all subdetectors to

reconstruct and identify individual particles produced in the event: charged hadrons,

neutral hadrons, photons, electrons, and muons, as shown in Figure 5.1. By leveraging the

full detector granularity and redundancy, PF improves energy and momentum resolution

compared to algorithms that rely on a single subsystem. This unified framework underpins

the construction of high-level objects, including jets and missing transverse momentum,

and enables robust pileup mitigation techniques.

Figure 5.1: Schematic of a transverse slice of the CMS detector, showing the signature of
various PF candidates in the subdetectors. Image courtesy: CERN Document Server

5.2.1 Particle Flow algorithm

The PF algorithm aims to reconstruct each final-state particle in the event by linking com-

plementary information from the CMS subdetectors. It begins with the reconstruction of

charged particle tracks in the inner tracker, which provide precise momentum measure-



58

ments and vertex associations. Calorimeter clusters are then reconstructed independently

in the electromagnetic (ECAL) and hadronic (HCAL) calorimeters. The algorithm subse-

quently links these elements to form PF candidates by identifying topological and spatial

correlations between tracks and calorimeter deposits.

Tracks matched to ECAL clusters with specific energy-momentum compatibility and

shower shape characteristics are identified as electrons. Tracks traversing the detector and

reaching the muon system are reconstructed as muons. Remaining tracks, not identified

as leptons, are considered charged hadrons. ECAL clusters not matched to any track

are interpreted as photons, and HCAL clusters without a matched track are classified

as neutral hadrons. This approach allows the PF algorithm to assign a particle type

and a four-momentum to each candidate with optimal resolution. The use of tracking

information for charged particles significantly improves the resolution of jet energies and

pmiss
T , particularly in events with high pileup.

5.2.2 Tracks and primary vertices

Charged particle tracks are reconstructed in the CMS inner tracker using a combinato-

rial track finding algorithm based on the Kalman Filter technique [90, 91]. The tracking

system, comprising silicon pixel and strip detectors, operates in a strong magnetic field of

3.8 T, allowing for precise measurement of the curvature of charged particle trajectories.

The tracking algorithm begins by seeding from hits in the pixel detector and progres-

sively adds compatible hits from subsequent tracker layers. Each candidate track is fit

to determine its momentum and trajectory parameters, with quality criteria applied to

suppress fake or poorly measured tracks. The tracking efficiency exceeds 95% for particles

with pT > 1 GeV within |η| < 2.4, with a fake rate of less than 1% under typical LHC

conditions.

Reconstructed tracks are then used to identify interaction vertices. The primary ver-

tex [92] is defined as the vertex with the highest
∑
p2T of its associated tracks, correspond-

ing to the hard-scatter interaction in most events. A deterministic annealing algorithm



59

is used to cluster tracks into vertex candidates, followed by a fit to determine the vertex

position and its uncertainty. The longitudinal resolution of the primary vertex position

is typically better than 20 µm for high-multiplicity events. Secondary vertices — arising

from heavy-flavor decays or displaced interactions — are also reconstructed using dis-

placed tracks, playing a critical role in b-tagging and searches for long-lived particles. The

association of each track to a vertex is essential for pileup mitigation and object isolation.

5.2.3 Electrons

Electrons are reconstructed by combining precise tracking information from the silicon

tracker with energy measurements in the ECAL [81, 93]. As charged leptons, elec-

trons leave a track in the inner detector, while their electromagnetic interactions lead

to the development of showers in the ECAL. Unlike muons, electrons undergo significant

bremsstrahlung when traversing the tracker material, resulting in energy loss and the

emission of photons along their trajectory. Electron reconstruction algorithms are there-

fore designed to recover this radiated energy and associate it with the primary electron

candidate.

Electron reconstruction begins with the identification of localized energy deposits in

the ECAL, known as superclusters, which are formed by clustering together adjacent

calorimeter crystals to capture both the primary electron energy and bremsstrahlung pho-

tons emitted in the tracker. Tracks reconstructed in the silicon tracker are then matched

to these superclusters, and a dedicated track fitting procedure is applied to account for en-

ergy loss due to bremsstrahlung. This combined approach enables accurate reconstruction

of the electron momentum over a wide kinematic range.

Electron identification relies on a multivariate discriminant that exploits the charac-

teristic features of electromagnetic showers and their associated tracks. Input variables in-

clude the shower shape in the ECAL, the quality of the track–cluster matching, the fraction

of energy deposited in the hadronic calorimeter, and variables sensitive to bremsstrahlung.

Several identification working points are defined, providing different trade-offs between ef-



60

ficiency and rejection of backgrounds from hadrons misidentified as electrons or from pho-

ton conversions. Typical working points achieve efficiencies of order 80–90% for prompt

electrons, with misidentification rates at the percent level.

Isolation requirements are often applied to further suppress backgrounds from non-

prompt electrons originating from heavy-flavor decays or from jets. The electron recon-

struction and identification efficiencies are measured in data using well-known resonant

processes, such as Z → e+e− decays, and corresponding scale factors are applied to sim-

ulated events to correct for residual differences between data and simulation. In analyses

targeting hadronic final states with missing transverse momentum, electrons are com-

monly used to define vetoes and control regions, enabling the suppression and estimation

of backgrounds from electroweak processes.

5.2.4 Muons

Muons are reconstructed in CMS by exploiting their ability to traverse the detector with

minimal energy loss, leaving characteristic ionizing tracks in both the inner tracking system

and the outer muon detectors. As a muon passes through the detector, it produces charged-

particle tracks in the silicon tracker and induces signals in the muon chambers embedded

in the steel return yoke of the solenoid. These complementary measurements enable robust

muon reconstruction over a wide range of transverse momentum and pseudorapidity [94].

CMS employs three complementary muon reconstruction approaches. Standalone

muons are reconstructed using only information from the muon system, where track seg-

ments are formed independently in the drift tubes (DT) in the barrel region and the cath-

ode strip chambers (CSC) in the endcaps, with additional timing information provided by

the resistive plate chambers (RPC). These segments are combined to form a standalone

track, providing coverage even when tracker information is unavailable. Tracker muons

are reconstructed by extrapolating tracks found in the silicon tracker to the muon system

and identifying compatible muon chamber segments. This approach benefits from the ex-

cellent momentum resolution of the tracker at low to intermediate transverse momentum.



61

Global muons are formed by performing a combined fit to matched tracker and standalone

muon tracks, resulting in optimal momentum resolution, particularly at high transverse

momentum.

Muon identification algorithms are applied to distinguish genuine prompt muons from

backgrounds arising from hadron decays in flight, punch-through, or detector noise. Iden-

tification criteria are based on track quality variables, the consistency between tracker and

muon system measurements, the number of matched muon stations, and the compatibility

of the reconstructed track with the primary interaction vertex. Several working points

(WPs) are defined, corresponding to different balances between efficiency and background

rejection. These working points typically achieve identification efficiencies above 95% for

prompt muons, with misidentification rates kept at the percent level or below, depending

on the chosen criteria.

In searches targeting hadronic final states with missing transverse momentum, muons

are often used to define vetoes or control regions, enabling the suppression and estimation

of backgrounds from electroweak processes such as W and Z boson production. Residual

differences in reconstruction and identification performance between data and simulation

are corrected using scale factors derived from data, ensuring accurate modeling of muon-

related efficiencies in simulated samples.

5.2.5 Jets

Jets are reconstructed as experimental proxies for quarks and gluons produced in the pp

collisions. Due to color confinement, partons emerging from the hard interaction undergo

hadronization and parton showering, which results in collimated sprays of particles that

deposit energy in the detector as illustrated in Figure 5.2.

Jet are reconstructed with the PF algorithm, with the charged hadrons reconstructed

primarily in the silicon tracker, while photons and neutral hadrons reconstructed using

energy deposits in the ECAL and HCAL.

ij = (ηi − ηj)2 + (ϕi − ϕj)2 is the angular separation

in η − ϕ space, and is a Lorentz invariant quantity. The diB is the distance between

the i particle and the beam pipe. The parameter R defines the size of the jet cone, with

R = 0.4 commonly used in CMS analyses and called AK4 jets. In regimes where the decay

products of heavy particles are highly collimated, such as boosted Higgs boson decays, a

larger distance parameter R = 0.8 (AK8) is employed.

The first step is to compute the distance in equation 5.1 for all particles, and locate

the smallest values dij and diB from the collection. If the smallest is of type dij , then a

new particle is formed by combining the i and j particles by adding their 4-momenta, with

subsequent removal of both i and j particles from the collection, and the new particle added

to the collection. If the smallest value is of type diB, then the i particle is considered a jet

and removed from the collection. After updating the collection of particles, the distances

are recalculated, and these steps are repeated until the list is exhausted. This way, the

algorithm ensures that the jets are preferentially seeded from the most energetic particles.



63

The defining feature of the anti-kT algorithm is that it preferentially clusters high pT

particles before softer ones. This causes soft radiation to be absorbed into nearby hard

jets, leading to stable, approximately conical boundaries that are largely insensitive to

additional soft activity from the underlying event or pileup. The algorithm is both infrared

and collinear safe, ensuring that the presence of soft emissions or collinear splittings does

not alter the reconstructed jet structure.

The reconstructed jet energies are corrected to account for detector effects and pileup.

Pileup mitigation is performed at the particle level prior to jet clustering. For AK4 jets,

charged hadrons not originating from the primary interaction vertex are removed using the

Charged Hadron Subtraction (CHS) technique. For larger-radius jets and jet substructure

observables, the PileUp Per Particle Identification (PUPPI) algorithm is employed, which

assigns weights to PF candidates based on their likelihood of originating from the primary

vertex. These techniques significantly improve jet kinematic resolution and reduce the

impact of pileup.

A sequence of jet energy corrections (JEC) is applied to both data and simulated

events. These corrections include an offset correction to remove the average contribution

from pileup, relative corrections to account for the pseudorapidity dependence of the

detector response, and absolute corrections to calibrate the jet energy scale as a function

of transverse momentum. Additional residual corrections are applied to data to account

for remaining differences between data and simulation. To ensure agreement between the

jet energy resolution observed in data and simulation, simulated jets are further smeared

according to the measured jet energy resolution.

5.2.6 B-tagged jets

Jets originating from bottom quarks (b jets) play a central role in analyses targeting

Higgs boson decays to bottom quark pairs. The identification of b jets exploits distinctive

properties of bottom-flavored hadrons that arise from the large mass of the bottom quark

and the structure of the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix. In particular,



64

the suppressed values of the relevant CKM matrix elements lead to comparatively long

lifetimes for b hadrons, allowing them to travel a measurable distance from the primary

interaction point before decaying.

As a consequence of their long lifetime, b hadrons typically decay at displaced loca-

tions within the inner tracking volume of the detector. Their decay products give rise to

tracks with large impact parameters relative to the primary vertex and, in many cases, to

well-resolved secondary vertices, as illustrated in Figure 5.3. These features provide pow-

erful experimental signatures that distinguish b jets from jets originating from light-flavor

quarks or gluons, whose decay products are predominantly consistent with originating

from the primary vertex.

65

The identification of b-jet is performed using multivariate algorithms that combine

information related to track impact parameters, reconstructed secondary vertices, and

global jet properties. For Run-2 analyses, the DeepJet algorithm is widely used. Deep-

Jet employs a deep neural network architecture that takes as input low-level information

from charged and neutral jet constituents, secondary vertex properties, and reconstructed

tracks. By exploiting correlations among these observables, the algorithm achieves im-

proved separation between b jets, charm jets, and light-flavor jets compared to earlier

approaches.

The output of the DeepJet algorithm is a continuous discriminator value, which can

be used to define working points corresponding to different efficiencies and misidentification

rates. Scale factors derived from data are applied to simulated events to correct for residual

differences in b-tagging performance between data and simulation. This is detailed in

Section 6.7.

Chapter 6

The Mono-Higgs analysis

6.1 Dark matter signal models

This doctoral work interprets the mono-Higgs(bb̄) search in two simplified models: the

baryonic-Z ′ model and the type-II two-Higgs-doublet model extended with a light pseu-

doscalar mediator (2HDM+a).

As discussed in Section 3.4, the baryonic-Z ′ model involves a massive vector mediator

(Z ′) which radiates an SM Higgs boson h and decays into a pair of DM candidates, χχ̄.

The mediator mass mZ′ and DM particle mass mχ are free parameters in the model and

are varied in this search. The coupling strength of Z ′ boson to SM quarks is fixed to

gq = 0.25 and that of Z ′ boson to DM particles is set to gχ = 1.

In the 2HDM+a model, the mono-Higgs signature arises from a scalar sector that

includes a heavy pseudoscalar A and a light pseudoscalar mediator a, in addition to the h

boson. When the mass hierarchymA > ma+mh is satisfied, the process A→ a+h becomes

kinematically allowed, with the lighter pseudoscalar subsequently decaying invisibly to a

pair of DM particles. The 2HDM+a framework offers a parameter space in which the

production cross section and kinematic distributions are governed by model parameters

such as the pseudoscalar masses mA, ma, the ratio of the vacuum expectation values tanβ,

and the sine of the mixing angle, sin θ. These model parameters are scanned over in the

analysis. The DM particle is assumed to have a mass of mχ = 10 GeV. The masses of the



68

heavy scalar, heavy pseudoscalar, and the two charged scalars are fixed to the same value,

, mH = mA = mH± [72].

6.2 Data and simulation

6.2.1 Data

We analyze the data collected by the CMS experiment corresponding to an integrated

luminosity of 101 fb−1, and was recorded in 2017 and 2018 data taking periods. A sta-

tistical combination is performed with the previous CMS analysis that uses 2016 data

corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36 fb−1. The collision data are split into pri-

mary datasets that are grouped depending on the class of HLT path that was triggered by

the event. The signal region and muon control regions use the primary dataset composed

of pmiss
T and Hmiss

T trigger, whereas the electron control regions use the dataset composed

of electron trigger.

6.2.2 Signal and background simulation

Signal and background contributions are modeled using Monte Carlo (MC) simulations.

All samples use NNPDF3.1 parton distribution functions (PDFs) at next-to-next-to-leading

order (NNLO) accuracy [96, 97]. The parton shower, hadronization, and the underlying

event simulation are provided by PYTHIA version 8.202 or later with the underlying

event tune CP5 [98]. The response of the CMS detector is simulated with the GEANT4

package [89]. Simulated events are reconstructed with the same software as used for data

events. All samples include the effects of additional pp interactions within the same or

nearby bunch crossings (pileup). Minimum bias interactions simulated with PYTHIA are

overlaid on the hard scattering interaction with a multiplicity distribution matching that

observed in the collider data.

The signal MC samples are produced centrally. These are generated at leading order

(LO) using MadGraph version 2.6.5 and interfaced with PYTHIA8 for hadronization.



69

The dominant background arises from the production of Z(νν̄)+jets and tt̄ pairs.

The Z(νν̄)+jets process is generated using MadGraph5 at next-to-LO (NLO) precision

in perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD). The lepton+jets decay of the tt̄ pair

constitutes the leading background contribution compared to dileptonic or hadronic de-

cays. All three tt̄ decay modes are simulated at NLO in pQCD using the POWHEG2.0

generator [99, 100, 101]. The pT spectra of top quarks in tt̄ data have been observed to

be significantly softer compared to MC simulations at LO or NLO, attributed to miss-

ing higher-order calculations. To mitigate this discrepancy, tt̄ events in simulation are

reweighted using a parametric function [102].

Subleading contributions arise fromW+jets, single top quark, and diboson (WW , ZZ,

and ZZ) processes. The W+jets background contributes to this analysis when the lepton

is not reconstructed or identified, or falls outside the detector acceptance. Events from

W+jets and Z(ℓℓ)+jets processes are simulated using the MadGraph5 generator at LO,

and the cross section is scaled to NLO accuracy in pQCD and electroweak (EW) correc-

tions. Event generation for the production of a single top quark in the t channel and in

association with a W boson is performed at NLO with the POWHEG generator. Diboson

background events are simulated at NLO in pQCD with the POWHEG or MadGraph5

generator.

The SM backgrounds with genuine Higgs bosons are produced via different processes:

gluon-gluon fusion, vector boson fusion, in association with a vector boson, or in associ-

ation with a pair of top quarks. These SM Higgs boson samples are all generated with

POWHEG at NLO in pQCD. The background from SM events composed uniquely of

jets produced through the strong interaction, referred to as QCD multijet events, is also

considered. These are generated at LO using MadGraph5.

The merging schemes employed for the MadGraph5 LO and NLO samples with the

parton shower model are MLM and FxFx, respectively.



70

Cross sections of the simulated processes are available at LO or NLO. In principle, we can

produce a large number of simulation events to obtain high statistical precision, although

these events need to be reweighted to correspond to the number of observable events in

data for a given center of mass energy. The weight applied to simulation events is,

6.3 Analysis strategy

The final state in this analysis, mono-Higgs(bb̄), is characterized by the presence of large

pmiss
T and an Higgs boson decaying to a pair of bottom quarks. Events containing an

isolated lepton or a photon are excluded. The Higgs boson is reconstructed in two mutually

exclusive categories, merged and resolved. Events with high-pT Higgs bosons are typically

captured in the merged category, whereas those with relatively low to moderate phT fall

into the resolved category. In the boosted regime, the Higgs boson decay products are

highly collimated, and can be reconstructed into a single large radius jet, also referred to

as a “FatJet”. In contrast, at lower phT, the decay products are well separated and the

particles from the bottom quark fragmentation are reconstructed into two small radius

AK4 jets. In the merged category, events containing a FatJet consistent with h → bb̄

decay and large pmiss
T are selected. Events failing the merged category selection are then

considered for the resolved category, which requires the presence of two b-tagged AK4 jets

recoiling against pmiss
T . Thus, the two categories are exclusive by construction.

Events with any loosely reconstructed tau lepton candidate with a pT greater than 20



71

GeV, |η| < 2.3 and |dz| < 0.2 are vetoed in the analysis. Events containing an isolated

photon candidate with pT greater than 20 GeV, |η| < 2.5, and passing loose identification

criteria with 90% efficiency are vetoed in all analysis regions.

6.4 Signal region event selections

The events in the SR are selected using a trigger with a pmiss
T threshold of 120 GeV, where

the online calculation of pmiss
T is based on all PF candidates reconstructed at the HLT.

The muon candidates identified by the PF algorithm are subtracted in this calculation.

As a result, events with high-pT muons are associated with large online pmiss
T , which allows

us to use the same trigger path to select events populating the single and di-muon CRs.

The pmiss
T trigger efficiency is around 90% at 200 GeV, and reaches 99% for 300 GeV and

above. Events in the electron CRs are selected using a single-electron trigger, with at least

one electron passing a pT threshold of 32 GeV. Events in the SR are required to pass the

pmiss
T requirement of 250 GeV in the merged and 200 GeV in resolved category.

To reduce background contribution from tt̄ andW +jets process in the SRs, the events

are required to have no isolated electrons (and muons) with pT > 10 (15) GeV, |η| ¡ 2.5

(2.4), passing loose quality criteria.

In the merged category SR, exactly one FatJet is required with pT > 200 GeV, |η| <

2.5, and soft-drop corrected mass (mSD) within 70 < mSD < 160, a window around the

boson mass that includes sidebands for the evaluation of background. To select events

where the FatJet originates from an h → bb̄ decay, the jet must pass the loose WP of

the ParticleNet-MD double-b algorithm. Furthermore, to reduce the tt̄ background

contribution, a selection is placed on the number of AK4 jets, , where we allow up to

two such jets with pT greater than 30 GeV that do not overlap with the Higgs candidate

FatJet, i.e. ∆R > 0.8. Events where the number of AK4 jets passing the loose DeepJet

WP (Nb-jets) is greater than zero are vetoed.

In the resolved-category SR, the two b-tagged AK4 jets must pass pT thresholds of

50 and 30 GeV. To reduce the tt̄ background by a factor of two while preserving high



72

acceptance for signal events, the h candidate, i.e., the “dijet” system formed by the two

(mbb̄) within 70–160 GeV. We impose a requirement similar to the one for the merged

category to suppress the tt̄ background: Njets ≤ 2, counting AK4 jets with pT > 30 GeV

within ∆R > 0.4 of either b-tagged jet forming the h candidate.

6.5 Background estimation

Now we turn our attention to the backgrounds. In this search for DM which is accompanied

by an SM Higgs boson decaying to a pair of b-quarks, the final state can be mimicked by

several SM processes, some of which have relatively high production cross section. The

dominant contribution is from top-quark pair production (tt̄) and vector boson production

in association with multiple jets (V + jets).

Z(νν̄) + jets is an irreducible background in this analysis. The lepton+jets decay of

the tt̄ pair constitutes the leading background contribution compared to the dileptonic

or hadronic decays. The W + jets background contributes to the SR when the lepton

is not reconstructed or identified, or falls outside the detector acceptance. Subleading

contributions arise fromW+jets, single top quark and diboson (ZZ,WZ,WW ) processes.

The associated production of the Higgs boson (WH, ZH) is also a background.

An accurate estimation of the SM background events in the SR is crucial for new physics

searches. If the background contribution is mismeasured or has large uncertainties, it can

wash out traces of signal. For this purpose, we design dedicated control regions (CRs)

which are enriched in certain background processes with large statistics. Additionally,

CRs are used to validate the MC simulations and the corrections applied to them. They

are designed to be devoid of signal events and any contamination if present is very small.

The dominant background processes, tt̄ and Z(νν̄) + jets are estimated separately in



74

each SR category using dedicated CRs. Single lepton CRs are used to constrain the tt̄

contribution, of which the lepton+jets decay is the most important, where the missed

lepton would serve as a source of pmiss
T . The dilepton CRs, enriched in Z(ℓℓ)+ jets events,

are used to constrain the Z(νν̄)+jets background which have similar kinematic properties.

The CRs are built by requiring exactly one or two well-reconstructed electrons or muons

which satisfy stringent quality criteria. These estimations rely on the distributions of data

and simulation in the CRs, and are linked to the SR via rate parameters. This strategy

is further discussed in Section 6.6. For the minor backgrounds, predictions from MC

simulation is used to predict their contributions in the SR.

single-lepton CRs—referred to as t(ℓ) CRs—and dilepton CRs—referred to as Z(ℓℓ) CRs—

defined separately for each SR category.

6.6 Signal extraction

The analysis is performed in two mutually exclusive categories (merged and resolved)

using a two-dimensional maximum likelihood fit. The observables are pmiss
T and the Higgs

boson candidate mass, mSD in the merged category and mbb̄ in the resolved category. The

Higgs boson candidate mass provides strong discrimination, as only the signal and well-

understood, subdominant SM backgrounds exhibit a resonant peak in this distribution. A

variable binning is used for pmiss
T in SRs (U in CRs) which is optimized for signal sensitivity

and tailored separately for each category. The bin edges are 250, 350, 500 GeV for the

merged category, and 200, 250, 290, 360, 420 GeV for the resolved category. Thus, the

signal is extracted using both the SRs and the corresponding CRs simultaneously in a

binned maximum likelihood fit.

For the dominant backgrounds, tt̄ and Z(νν̄) + jets, the Higgs boson candidate mass

distribution in each pmiss
T window of the SRs is tied to the corresponding U window in

the CRs via a scale factor whose systematic uncertainty is accounted for with a nuisance



78

parameter in the fit. For each category, the electron and muon CRs are combined appro-

priately to form a single CR for each background estimated from data. The contributions

from other background processes are taken directly from MC simulation, with their nomi-

nal expected yield obtained after applying all event selections and normalizing them to the

integrated luminosity times their respective theoretical cross sections. The fit to the data

determines the background post-fit yields in each bin, which are obtained as the pre-fit

yields adjusted by the post-fit values of the scale factors through their associated nuisance

parameters. The systematic uncertainties, many of which are shape-based, account for

experimental sources, such as jet energy scale and resolution, b tagging, lepton identifica-

tion and trigger efficiencies, as well as theoretical uncertainties affecting the background

and signal distributions. The shape-based systematic uncertainties further ensure that

any residual mismodeling is accounted for in the total uncertainty.

The final free parameter in the fit is the signal strength modifier µ, which controls the

signal normalization relative to the theoretical cross section for a given signal hypothesis.

The best fit background model, and the best fit signal strength are simultaneously obtained

by maximizing the likelihood fit across the two categories, all SRs and CRs, and all data-

taking periods.

6.7.1 Pileup

Pileup interactions at the LHC are frequent and must be properly modeled in MC sim-

ulations. The simulated samples are generated with a distribution of number of pileup

interactions which may not match the recorded collision data due to changes in beam

conditions over the period of data taking. This difference is corrected by reweighting the

simulated samples, where the event weight depends on the number of true interaction

vertices in MC. The inelastic pp cross section in Run-2 is measured to be 69.2 mb and an

uncertainty of ±4.6% in this measurement is used to calculate the systematic uncertainty

on the event weight.

6.7.2 L1 prefiring

The 2017 data taking period was affected by “prefiring”. The gradual timing shift of

ECAL was not properly propagated to the L1 trigger primitives (TP) which resulted in

a large fraction of high η TP to be incorrectly associated to the previous bunch crossing.

As the Level-1 rules do not allow two consecutive bunch crossings to fire, this can cause

events to self veto if a large amount of ECAL energy is found in 2 < η < 3. For jets

with pT of several hundred GeVs and very high η values (2.75 to 3), the prefiring rates

go above 50%. This effect leads to an overall decrease of the trigger efficiency. This effect

can also be found in muon systems, where the bunch crossing assignment of the muon is

incorrect because of limited time resolution of the muon detectors. To reflect this in the

simulations, a procedure is provided to compute the probability for an event to not prefire

which is applied as event weight to the MC simulations. In nanoAOD, this is provided in

the L1PreFiring branch with the nominal and up/down variations which are obtained by

shifting all prefiring probabilities ±1 standard deviations.



80

6.7.3 HEM issue in 2018

During the data taking in 2018, the power supply of two HCAL modules were not func-

tioning as expected. For run numbers 319077 and above, the HCAL deposits were not

recorded in the η region between -3.0 and -1.3 and ϕ region between -1.57 and -0.87. This

corresponds to the later part of era 2018B and full of 2018C and 2018D. In this region, jet

reconstruction was affected, and as a consequence so was the calculation of the missing

transverse energy.

To mitigate the effect of this detector issue in our analysis, we veto the event if any

jet is found in the affected η and ϕ regions in the data event. To mimic this feature in

the MC simulated events, we first calculate the luminosity of the affected runs and the

proportion of the affected luminosity to the total recorded luminosity in 2018 data. For

the affected proportion of events in MC simulation, which was 64.77%, the same criteria

is used to veto events if any jet is found in the HEM affected region.

For the electron control regions this veto strategy was found to be insufficient. An

additional number of events are vetoed if an electron is present in the HEM affected

region. Figure Z shows the electron η − ϕ map in 2018 data with the jet based only (left)

and jet and electron based (right) veto.

For analyses targeting similar topology (jets and large pmiss

6.7.10 Uncertainties

All systematic uncertainties affecting the simulated processes (signal and background) in

the analysis regions are treated as nuisance parameters within the likelihood function.

These parameters influence either the normalization or the shape of the pmiss
T (U) dis-

tribution for a given process in the SR (CR) and are constrained in the simultaneous

fit.

Uncertainties that do not affect the shape of the distribution, or are uniformly dis-

tributed are treated as normalization uncertainties and incorporated using log-normal

distributions. Those having nonuniform variations are treated as shape uncertainties and

are incorporated by means of Gaussian prior distributions. Experimental and theoretical

sources of systematic uncertainty considered in this search are described below.

• The pmiss
T trigger efficiency is measured using single-muon events passing the

single-muon trigger with a pT threshold of 27 (24) GeV for data recorded in 2017

(2018). It is parametrized as a function of the U variable, and the corresponding

data-to-simulation correction factors are applied to the simulation in the SRs and

the single-muon and dimuon CRs.



88

• The electron trigger efficiency is parametrized as a function of the electron pT

and η. An associated uncertainty of 1–2% is assigned to both the trigger scale

factors.

• Lepton reconstruction and identification uncertainties are evaluated and in-

corporated as a function of pT and η. The systematic uncertainties related to muon

identification and isolation have a normalization effect of less than 1%. For elec-

trons, the systematic uncertainties associated with reconstruction (identification)

have a normalization effect of 1–2 (1–5)%. An uncertainty of 6 (2)% is assigned to

the tau lepton (photon) veto efficiency across all analysis regions.

• The integrated luminosities for the 2016, 2017, and 2018 data-taking years have

1.2–2.5% individual uncertainties, while the overall uncertainty for the 2016–2018

period is 1.6%. A normalization uncertainty of 2.5% is applied to all background

processes taken directly from the MC simulations [105, 106, 107, 108].

• Pileupmodeling is addressed by reweighting the signal and background MC samples

such that the number of true pileup interactions in simulation matches the pileup

profile observed in data. The latter is determined using integrated luminosity per

bunch crossing and assuming the total inelastic cross-section of 69.2mb [109]. The

systematic uncertainty from the pileup re-weighting is evaluated by varying the total

inelastic cross-section by ±4.6%.

• During the 2017 data-taking period, a gradual shift in the timing of the inputs of

the ECAL L1 trigger in the η > 2.0 region caused a trigger inefficiency, denoted as

“prefiring” [85]. The trigger missed between 10 and 20% of the events containing

an electron (of pT ≳ 50) or a jet (of pT ≳ 100) in the 2.5 < η < 3.0 range, the

exact loss depending on the pT and η of the trigger object. Correction factors were

computed from data and applied to the acceptance evaluated by simulation. The

shape-based uncertainty for L1 prefiring has a normalization effect of 0.5–1%.

• The JES corrections depend on jet pT and η, and the uncertainties are split into



89

11 independent sources accounting for different experimental effects [110]. These

systematic uncertainties are considered for all simulation-based processes, with a

shape effect ranging from 0.1 to 5%. Differences in the JER between data and

simulation are accounted for by smearing the pT of jets in MC samples. The smearing

factors and their uncertainties depend on the jet η. The shape-based uncertainty is

assigned to all simulated processes, with an effect of around 4%. The change in the

jet momentum due to JER smearing is propagated to the pmiss
T computation.

• The efficiency of the DeepJet [111, 112] b tagging algorithm is parametrized as a

function of jet pT, η, and flavor, and is applied to AK4 b jets making the h candidate

in the resolved category. Discrepancies between data and simulation are corrected for

using data-to-simulation correction factors. Shape-based uncertainties are computed

separately for genuine b jets and misidentified b jets, with an average shape effect

of 5%. For the merged category, an additional uncertainty in the ParticleNet-MD

double-b tagging efficiency is applied to AK8 jets as a function of their pT, with

an average shape effect of around 2% [113, 114].

Most experimental uncertainties are specific to each data set and are thus assumed

to be uncorrelated between different data-taking periods. The uncertainties related to

integrated luminosity, JES and JER, as well as those related to b tagging are partially

correlated between the data-taking periods, which is implemented by splitting the total

uncertainty into its correlated and uncorrelated components.

To mitigate discrepancies between the data and MC simulations in the pT spectra

of the top quarks in tt̄ events, a parametric function is used to reweight the simulation.

The uncertainty associated with this correction is estimated by comparing weighted and

unweighted results, leading to a shape effect of around 7%.

Shape uncertainties for the LO-to-NLO scale factors obtained forW+jets, Z(νν̄)+jets,

and Z(ℓℓ) + jets processes [104] are considered to account for the missing higher-order

corrections with QCD and EW terms. These shape uncertainties range from 5 to 20%,

depending on the category, process, and boson pT.



90

Uncertainties in the PDFs and those due to variations in the renormalization and

factorization scales (µR and µF) impact both the shape and cross section of simulated

processes. The PDF uncertainty is evaluated by reweighting simulated events using the

set of PDF replicas from the NNPDF3.1 PDFs, following the PDF4LHC recommenda-

tions [115]. The envelope of variations is taken as the systematic uncertainty, with a

typical effect of 3–6% depending on the process and category. Scale uncertainties are

estimated by individually varying the µR and µF scales up and down by a factor of two,

with the exception of simultaneously varying both up or down. The resulting uncertainty

is 10–20%, and is treated as uncorrelated for the signal as well as the various background

processes. These uncertainties are treated as correlated across categories and data-taking

eras.

For background processes taken directly from the simulations, a normalization uncer-

tainty of 10% is assigned to the single top quark process, 20% to the W + jets process,

and 30% to the diboson process. These values are chosen based on existing experimental

constraints [116, 117, 118, 119]. For the signal process, a normalization uncertainty of

10% is assigned. A cross section uncertainty of 5% is assigned to the SM Higgs process.

These uncertainties are correlated across categories and data-taking eras.

The MC bin-by-bin statistical uncertainties are handled using the CMS statistical tool

Combine, which employs the “Barlow-Beeston-lite” technique. A Poisson threshold of 10

events is set, such that for MC event counts exceeding 10, the uncertainty is modeled with

a Gaussian distribution, while for counts below 10, a Poisson distribution is used to model

per-process uncertainties in that bin.

The results based on the data set analyzed in this paper are further combined with

the results from an earlier analysis based on data collected in 2016. The combination is

performed by running a combined likelihood fit across all the analysis regions in all data

sets. For this purpose, the uncertainty in integrated luminosity is partially correlated,

and the PDF uncertainty is fully correlated between data-taking eras. The remaining

uncertainty sources are treated as uncorrelated in the final combined fit.

6.8 Statistical inference

Statistical inference is the final and crucial step in an analysis to interprets the experimen-

tal data. It uses a statistical model which provides a complete mathematical framework

to draw conclusions about the underlying physics process based on the observed data.

The model encodes the probabilistic dependence of the observed quantities on the model

parameters, which include parameters of interest (POI) and nuisance parameters. The

former are quantities like cross section of a process, signal strength, or mass of a new

particle. The latter are parameters that are needed to explain the observed data, such as

experimental or theory uncertainties.

The statistical analysis is designed to test for the presence of a signal compatible with

mono-Higgs signature and to quantify the level of agreement between the observed data



92

and the SM background expectation. This is formulated as a hypothesis testing problem,

in which a background-only hypothesis H0 (µ = 0) is compared to a signal+background

hypothesis H1 (µ > 0). The goal of the analysis is to assess whether the observed data are

consistent with H0 or whether there is sufficient evidence to reject it in favor of H1. The

analysis uses a likelihood-based framework with the CMS COMBINE tool [120], which

provides an implementation of the likelihood inference with a consistent treatment of the

systematic uncertainties.

To enhance the sensitivity of the search, the statistical inference is based on a fit to

the unrolled Higgs candidate mass distributions - mSD in merged category and mbb̄ in

resolved category, and sliced into several pmiss
T regions. This approach of using multiple

pmiss
T regions takes advantage of the different kinematic behavior of signal and background

processes: while the dominant SM backgrounds tend to populate the low pmiss
T regime, a

potential mono-Higgs signal is expected to produce harder pmiss
T spectra. Performing the

fit simultaneously across all pmiss
T slices allows the analysis to exploit both the shape of

the mass distribution and the event migration across pmiss
T regions, thereby increasing the

overall discrimination power compared to a single inclusive fit.

The likelihood model includes independent rate (normalization) parameters for each

pmiss
T region, with three regions in the merged category and five in resolved category. Sep-

arate sets of these parameters are introduced for the two dominant background processes,

tt̄ and Z(νν̄) + jets, which are allowed to float freely in the combined fit.

The transfer of background predictions from the CRs to the SR is implemented using

the rateParam feature of the COMBINE tool [120, 121]. For each dominant background

process and each pmiss
T bin, a floating normalization parameter is introduced and linked

simultaneously to the corresponding process in the SR and the associated CR. Concretely,

the expected yield of a given background process in the SR is expressed as,

Nbkg
SR = κ×Nbkg

CR × µbkg (6.9)

where Nbkg
CR is the MC prediction in the CR, κ is the MC-derived transfer factor that



93

accounts for the kinematic and acceptance differences between the CR and SR, and µbkg

is the floating normalization parameter shared between the two regions. The transfer

factor κ encodes the ratio of the SR to CR yields as predicted by simulation, and absorbs

differences in selection efficiency, acceptance, and process composition between the two

regions. By constraining µbkg through the data in the CR, the background prediction in

the SR is effectively data-driven, reducing the dependence on the absolute normalization

of the MC simulation. A simple overview of the rateParam is illustrated in Figure 6.9.

Figure 6.9: A schematic view of usage of rateParam to connect the dominant background
distributions in SR to the dedicated CRs.

This approach is applied independently for each pmiss
T bin and for each background

process, with separate rateParam instances for tt̄ and Z(νν̄)+ jets. The single-lepton CR

primarily constrains the tt̄ normalization, while the di-lepton CR provides the dominant

constraint on the Z(νν̄) + jets background. Sources of systematic uncertainty that affect

the transfer factor κ, such as jet energy corrections, b-tagging efficiencies, and theoretical

modeling uncertainties — are propagated as correlated nuisance parameters across the

SR and CR, ensuring that the extrapolation uncertainty is consistently accounted for in

the fit. This ensures a coherent description of each background process across the full

phase space. By allowing the background rates to vary independently in each kinematic



94

regime, the fit can absorb residual mismodeling in the overall yields while preserving the

shape information that is critical for distinguishing signal-like events from background-like

events.

The likelihood function is constructed as the product of Poisson probabilities over all

analysis regions, including the merged and resolved category SRs, and the corresponding

single and di-lepton CRs. The product also involves all the analysis bins in pmiss
T and the

Higgs candidate mass distributions. For a given bin i, the expected number of events is,

λi(µ, θ) = µsi(θ) + bi(θ) (6.10)

where si and bi are the expected signal and background yields in bin i, with θ being the

set of nuisance parameters encoding the systematic uncertainties. The full likelihood is,

L(µ, θ) =

where di is the observed number of events in bin i, and yk are the prior constraint terms

for each nuisance parameter θk, which are typically Gaussian or log-normal and reflect the

estimated size of the associated uncertainty.

The systematic uncertainties enter the likelihood through their effect on both the

normalization and shape of the expected distributions. For each source of uncertainty,

an “up” and “down” variation is provided and its impact on si and bi is interpolated as

a function of the corresponding nuisance parameter. Experimental uncertainties include

jet energy corrections, b-tagging efficiency, etc which are shape-based, while theoretical

uncertainties include PDF, renormalization and factorization scale, which account for the

cross section normalization and modeling of background processes.

In order to maximize the likelihood, we “profile” over the nuisance parameters. This

refers to finding the values that maximizes the likelihood for each value of the POI. The



95

profiled likelihood then is,

L(µ) = L(µ, θ̂µ) = maxθ L(µ, θ) (6.12)

We use the negative log of the likelihood (NLL) to avoid small or large values, and

assuming µ̂ to be the value which minimizes the NLL. Subtracting the value at the minima,

we get,

−∆lnL = −lnL(µ, θ̂µ)− (−lnL(µ̂, θ̂))

and −2∆lnL is the profile likelihood ratio, and used as a test statistic for hypothesis

testing. Larger values of the test statistic indicate greater incompatibility between the

data and the hypothesis being tested.

Here, θ̂µ denotes the values of nuisance parameters that maximize the likelihood for

a fixed µ, and (µ̂, θ̂) are the unconditional maximum-likelihood estimators. This test

statistic quantifies the compatibility of the observed data with a given signal hypothesis

µ. In the absence of a significant excess over the SM background prediction, the results

are interpreted in terms of upper limits on the signal strength µ.

The p-value is then defined as the probability, under the assumption of H0 of obtaining

a value of the test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed in data,

p0 =

∫ ∞

qobs

f(q|H0)dq (6.14)

where f(q|H0) is the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothe-

sis, typically obtained via asymptotic approximations or pseudo-experiments (toy MC). A

small p-value indicates that the observed data would be unlikely under H0, and is inter-

preted as evidence against H0. In particle physics, the conventional threshold for claiming



96

a discovery is: p0 ≤ 2.87× 10−7, corresponding to a local significance of 5σ.

Closely related to hypothesis testing is the construction of confidence intervals [122,

123], which provide a range of parameter values that are compatible with the observed

data at a specified confidence level. In the frequentist interpretation, a confidence interval

[µlower, µupper] at confidence level 1−α, is defined such that over an ensemble of repeated

experiments, the true value of the parameter µ would be contained within the interval in

a fraction 1 − α of the cases. It is important to note that this is a statement about the

interval construction procedure, rather than a probabilistic statement about the true value

itself. In practice, confidence intervals are obtained by inverting the hypothesis test: the

interval is defined as the set of all values of µ for which the hypothesis Hµ is not rejected

at significance level α, i.e. all values for which CLs(µ) > α.

Before looking at the collision data, we can create approximations of what we expect

to see. An Asimov dataset is used to evaluate expected sensitivities and constraints, where

the observed yield di is replaced by the expected values under a given hypothesis. This is

because under the Asimov dataset, the maximum likelihood estimation of µ equals the true

injected value by construction, which is what makes the expected limits well-defined. This

allows us to study the expected behavior of the fit, and is free from statistical fluctuations.

We calculate the significance and expected limits using the Asimov dataset. Along with

the expected limits, we also find a ±1σ and ±2σ band from the expected value using the

Asimov dataset. This can help assess how well the observed data matches the expectations.

The same likelihood model is then fitted to real data. The fits are performed simultane-

ously across all analysis regions and bins. Nuisance parameters corresponding to common

sources of uncertainty are shared across regions, and the normalization parameters for

dominant background processes are linked between control and signal regions, allowing

the data in background-enriched CRs to constrain the background predictions in the SRs.

If the observed data are found to be consistent with the background-only hypothesis,

then upper limits are set on the signal strength µ using the modified frequentist [124] CLs



97

criteria. The CLs is defined as,

CLs =
CLs+b

CLb
(6.15)

where CLs+b and CLb are the confidence levels for the signal+background and background-

only hypotheses, respectively. A signal hypothesis is excluded at 95% confidence level if

CLs < 0.05.

The quality of the fit and the modeling of the background processes are assessed

by comparing the post-fit predicted yields to the observed data in all analysis regions.

Following the simultaneous maximum likelihood fit to data under the background-only

hypothesis (µ = 0), the nuisance parameters and background normalization factors are

adjusted to their post-fit values, and the resulting predicted distributions are compared

to the observed data in both the signal and control regions.

The post-fit mSD and mbb̄ distributions in the merged and resolved SRs are shown in

Figures 6.10 for each pmiss
T slice. The post-fit distributions show good agreement between

the data and the background prediction across the full range of the Higgs candidate mass

and across all pmiss
T regions, with no significant localized excess observed. The dominant

background contributions from tt̄ and Z(νν̄)+jets are also seen, illustrating how each pro-

cess contributes across the different kinematic regimes. The fitted normalization factors for

these processes are found to be consistent with unity within uncertainties, indicating that

the pre-fit MC predictions provide a reasonable description of the data after accounting

for the systematic uncertainties.

The corresponding post-fit distributions in the single-lepton and di-lepton CRs are

shown in Figures 6.11 – 6.14. The good agreement observed in the CRs confirms that the

rateParam-based transfer factors are well-constrained by the data, and that the extrapo-

lation of background predictions into the SR is robust.

The upper limits are obtained using the asymptotic approximation [125] of the test

statistic distributions, as implemented in COMBINE. While the fit is performed internally

in terms of the signal strength modifier µ, the results are expressed as 95% CL upper limits
