6.9 Interpretation of search results

The results of the mono-Higgs search are interpreted in the context of simplified models of

dark matter production associated with an SM Higgs boson decaying to a pair of bottom

quarks. The experimental outcome is expressed in terms of 95% CL upper limits on

the signal production cross section. These limits are also translated into exclusions on

the model parameters, allowing the results to be compared directly with the theoretical

expectations.

The first model considered is the baryonic-Z ′ model, where a new massive gauge boson

mediates the interaction between the SM quarks and the dark matter particles. In this

framework, the relevant free parameters are the mediator mass mZ′ and the dark matter

mass mχ, while the coupling of Z ′ to quarks and DM particles are fixed to benchmark

values, as discussed in Section 6.1. The experimental limits on the mono-Higgs production

cross section are compared to the predicted cross sections for different points in the (mZ′ ,

mχ) plane, and parameter points for which the predicted signal exceeds the observed 95%

CL upper limits are excluded. The resulting exclusion is presented as a two-dimensional

contour in the mediator–DM mass plane.

The second class of models considered is the two-Higgs-doublet model with an addi-

tional pseudoscalar mediator (2HDM+a), which extends the Higgs sector of the SM and

introduces a portal between visible and dark sectors. In this scenario, the phenomenol-

ogy is governed by several parameters, including the masses of the light and heavier

pseudoscalars ma and mA, the mixing angle between the CP -odd weak eigenstates sin θ,

and the ratio of the vacuum expectation values of the two Higgs doublets tanβ. Rather

than scanning the full multi-dimensional parameter space, the interpretation is performed

through a set of one-dimensional exclusions, in which one parameter is varied at a time

while the others are fixed to benchmark values.

For both models, the theoretical predictions for the signal cross sections are computed

for each parameter point and compared to the experimental 95% CL upper limits obtained

from the statistical analysis. Parameter regions in which the predicted cross section lies



105

above the observed limit are excluded at 95% CL.

Figure 6.15 shows the exclusion limit at 95% CL on the signal cross section σh+DM, as

a two-dimensional scan over mZ′ and mχ. In this scan, the coupling between the mediator

and SM quarks is fixed to gq = 0.25, and the coupling between the mediator and DM

particles is fixed to gχ = 1. For mχ = 1 GeV, values of mZ′ below 2.25 TeV (2.35 TeV

expected) are excluded. Masses of DM particles up to 550 GeV (600 GeV expected) are

excluded for mZ′ = 1.25 TeV.

Figure 6.15: Exclusion limits at 95% CL on the signal cross section σh+DM for the
baryonic-Z ′ model as a function of mZ′ and mχ. The coupling parameters are fixed
to gq = 0.25 and gχ = 1. The areas within the solid black and red contours represent
the exclusion regions where the theoretical cross sections are larger than the observed and
expected experimental limits, respectively. The areas within the dashed and dotted red
contours show the excluded regions at ±1 and ±2 standard deviations from the expected
limits, respectively [103].

Compared to the previous result in Ref. [126] with the 2016 data set, the maximal

exclusion limit in terms of mZ′ is improved by 650 GeV (500 GeV expected) for mχ = 1

GeV. The higher luminosity data contributes around 300 GeV of expected improvement,

with the additional 200 GeV of expected exclusion coming from the improved identification

of boosted h→ bb̄ decays with the latest tagging algorithms.

Figure 6.16 shows the observed and expected exclusion limits at 95% CL on the signal



106

cross section σh+DM for four one-dimensional parameter scans (ma, mA, sin θ, and tanβ).

For the ma scan (upper left plot), the fixed parameters are mA = 1000 GeV, sin θ = 0.35,

and tanβ = 1. Light pseudoscalar masses below 360 GeV are excluded. For the mA scan

(upper right plot), the fixed parameters are ma = 350 GeV, sin θ = 0.35, and tanβ = 1,

with heavy pseudoscalar masses between 850 and 1300 GeV excluded. For the sin θ scan

(lower left plot), the fixed parameters are ma = 200 GeV, mA = 600 GeV, and tanβ = 1,

with sin θ values between 0.15 and 0.95 excluded. The variation of sin θ leads to both rate

and shape changes in the pmiss
T spectrum, where the strong sensitivity is a result of the

interplay of resonant and non-resonant contributions. The process pp → A → ha → hχχ̄

scales as sin θ cos2(θ) and the process pp → ha → hχχ̄ shows a sin θ dependence, as

detailed in Ref. [71]. Finally, for the tanβ scan (lower right plot), the fixed parameters

are ma = 200 GeV, mA = 600 GeV, and sin θ = 0.35, where tanβ values below 4.2 are

excluded by this analysis. As long as mχ < ma/2, the decay is kinematically allowed, with

very little dependence of either the rate or pmiss
T spectrum on mχ. We choose a benchmark

value mχ = 10 GeV [71].

Motivated by Ref. [71], different sets of model parameters are tested, corresponding to

(mA,ma) = (1000, 350) GeV (Fig. 6.16 upper plots) and (600, 200) GeV (Fig. 6.16 lower

plots). These choices probe distinct regions of phase space, resulting in signal events with

different kinematic features. In particular, the former configuration yields higher pmiss
T ,

and together with different production cross sections, these variations result in differences

between the observed and expected exclusion limits.

Each plot represents a slice through the multi-dimensional parameter space, keeping

the other parameters fixed at benchmark values. The search exhibits the strongest sensi-

tivity in regions where the pseudoscalar mediator ’a’ is light, enhancing the mono-Higgs

production rate, and for moderate values of sin θ that maximize the coupling between

the visible and dark sectors. Conversely, very small or very large mixing angles reduce

the effective coupling and therefore the expected signal yield, leading to weaker exclusion

limits.

tested to probe distinct regions of phase space. Mass points below the solid red line are
excluded [103].

In both models, the 95% CL upper limits on the signal production cross section are

indicated alongside the exclusion regions. The limits are derived from the observed data,

with expected limits and their ±1σ and ±2σ bands provided to quantify the impact

of statistical fluctuations and systematic uncertainties. The observed limits generally



108

track the median expected limits, demonstrating that the data are consistent with the

background-only hypothesis and that no significant excess is observed in any kinematic

region or category.

The results also illustrate how different analysis categories contribute to the overall

sensitivity. The merged and resolved SRs provide complementary coverage of the kine-

matic spectrum: the merged category dominates sensitivity at high pmiss
T , where the Higgs

decay products are collimated, while the resolved category is more sensitive at lower miss-

ing transverse momentum. The combination of both categories in a single simultaneous

fit allows maximizing exclusion power and extending the reach of the search to a broader

range of signal kinematics than either category alone could achieve.

Finally, the interpretation demonstrates the power of mono-Higgs searches to probe

physics beyond the Standard Model. The baryonic-Z ′ model exclusions constrain mediator

masses up to 2.25 TeV for light dark matter, while the 2HDM+a limits provide meaningful

constraints on the pseudoscalar mass and mixing parameters. Although no evidence for

dark matter production is observed, the derived limits significantly restrict the available

parameter space for these models and complement other direct and indirect dark matter

searches, providing valuable guidance for both theory and future experimental strategies.



109

Conclusion

A search for dark matter (DM) produced in association with a Standard Model Higgs

boson decaying to a bottom quark-antiquark pair has been presented. The analysis is

based on proton-proton collision data collected in 2017 and 2018 by the CMS experiment

at
√
s = 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 101 fb−1. The search has

been performed in merged and resolved categories to cover a wide range of Lorentz boosts

of the Higgs boson. The signal is extracted using a simultaneous maximum likelihood fit

to the signal and control regions by combining the two categories. The observed data

agree with the Standard Model background prediction, indicating no evidence for new

physics. The results are statistically combined with an earlier search using 2016 data,

corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb−1.

The full 2016–2018 results have been interpreted in two simplified models, the baryonic-Z ′

model where a high mass resonance (Z ′) decays to a pair of DM particles and a Higgs

boson, and the 2HDM+a model where a heavy pseudoscalar couples to a Higgs boson and

a lighter pseudoscalar that decays to a pair of DM particles. Exclusion limits are set on

the model parameters at 95% confidence level. For the baryonic-Z ′ model, mediator Z ′

masses up to 2.25 TeV are excluded for a DM mass of 1 GeV, and DM particle masses

up to 550 GeV are excluded for a 1.25 TeV Z ′ particle. In the 2HDM+a framework,

light pseudoscalar masses ma below 360 GeV are excluded for a heavy pseudoscalar mass

mA of 1000 GeV, and mA masses between 850 and 1300 GeV are excluded for ma of 350

GeV. For the other model parameters, sin θ values between 0.15 and 0.95 are excluded,

while tanβ values less than 4.2 are excluded. These results improve upon the previously



110

existing LHC limits owing to the larger integrated luminosity and improved identification

of h→ bb̄ decay.



111

Future prospects

The mono-Higgs(bb̄) search presented in this thesis establishes an analysis framework for

probing dark matter produced in association with a Standard Model Higgs boson. Looking

forward, several developments offer opportunities to further improve the sensitivity.

CMS Run-3 search for mono-Higgs(bb)

A natural next step is the extension of this analysis strategy to Run-3 data, which is

currently underway. The increased center of mass energy (13.6 TeV) and the growing

integrated luminosity provide a substantially larger dataset, enabling improved statistical

precision and access to previously inaccessible regions of parameter space. In parallel,

several methodological improvements are being pursued to enhance the sensitivity of the

analysis. These include the use of the latest b-tagging algorithms developed within the

CMS experiment, which offer improved discrimination between heavy- and light-flavor

jets, as well as the application of b-jet mass regression techniques to achieve better mass

resolution of the reconstructed Higgs boson candidate. The second is particularly useful

for the events in the resolved category which target low to moderate pT Higgs bosons.

Furthermore, the incorporation of state-of-the-art machine learning approaches, such as a

multivariate discriminant is expected to provide additional gains in signal-to-background

separation, thereby further improving the overall sensitivity of this search.



112

Prospects at a high energy muon collider

Despite the sensitivity achieved at LHC, these searches are bound by energy reach and

large QCD backgrounds in the pp environment which impose stringent event selections

that erode signal acceptance for large DM mass hypotheses. A muon collider operating

at high energy (few TeVs) offers a qualitatively different environment. As muons are

fundamental particles, the full center-of-mass energy is available for the collision. Together

with a projected integrated luminosity of 10 ab−1, allows a muon collider to probe DM

and mediator masses well into the TeV regime, which is theoretically well-motivated but

largely inaccessible at the LHC.

The motivation for targeting DM masses in the multi-TeV range is not only that it

represents unexplored territory, but there exists a specific and well-motivated theoretical

target rooted in the thermal relic hypothesis. If DM was produced thermally in the

early universe and its abundance was set by freeze-out, the observed relic density fixes

the thermally averaged annihilation cross section to ⟨σv⟩ ≈ 3× 10−26cm3/s, a result that

holds to leading order independently of the DM mass [127]. For a DM particle that couples

to the SM through electroweak interactions, this corresponds to DM masses ranging from

O(100) GeV up to a few TeV depending on the model and the electroweak representation,

for example, a pure wino satisfies the relic density at ∼ 3 TeV, and a pure higgsino at

∼ 1 TeV. An absolute upper bound on the thermal relic mass comes from the requirement

that the annihilation cross section not violate perturbative unitarity [128], which sets a

model-independent ceiling near 100 TeV. Both the baryonic-Z ′ and 2HDM+a models can

accommodate DM in this range as thermal relics, and a multi-TeV muon collider can probe

much of it directly in the mono-Higgs channel.

The HL-LHC, with its projected 3000 fb−1 data at
√
s = 14 TeV is expected to

improve on Run-3 constraints, but may not reach the multi-TeV DM mass range. A muon

collider, however, can enter this regime, and directly test whether DM is a thermal WIMP

at masses where the WIMP hypothesis is most natural. Moreover, a muon collider offers

a unique opportunity to measure the model parameters rather than just set limits.



113

Direct detection experiments face two structural limitations that define the boundary

of what they can ultimately achieve, and a muon collider offers a complementary path

around both. The first is the astrophysical neutrino background [129]. Solar neutrinos

dominate the background at WIMP masses below 10 GeV, while atmospheric neutrinos

and the diffuse supernova neutrino background become relevant at higher WIMP masses.

Once the neutrino floor is reached, additional exposure yields diminishing returns, as the

sensitivity improves only as the square root of exposure rather than linearly. A muon

collider produces DM particles in a controlled collider experiment free of astrophysical

neutrino backgrounds, and is therefore not subjected to this limitation.

The second limitation is kinematic. The energy deposited by a DM particle scattering

off a xenon nucleus at the galactic halo velocity v ∼ 10−3c is typically a few keV, and for

WIMP masses much larger than the xenon nuclear mass (mXe ≈ 122 GeV), the nuclear

recoil spectrum shape becomes nearly independent of the WIMP mass. This means that

direct detection cannot use the observed recoil distribution to determine the DM mass in

the multi-TeV regime (mχ ≫ mXe). Additionally, because the local DM number density

scales as ρlocal/mχ for fixed local density ρlocal ≈ 0.3 GeV/cm3, the event rate per unit

detector mass falls at large mχ even at fixed spin-independent cross section, reducing

sensitivity to heavy DM even before the neutrino floor is reached. At a collider, however,

the DM is produced with kinematics determined by the beam energy. The DM mass

can be inferred from the pmiss
T spectrum and the kinematic endpoints of the visible recoil

system. Although this inference is model-dependent as it relies on assumptions about the

production topology and mediator structure, a collider measurement provides a direct and

qualitatively different handle on DM mass that direct detection cannot replicate in the

multi-TeV regime.

The search for DM with mono-Higgs signature at CMS experiment presented in this

thesis represents the current state-of-the-art at the LHC. A well-motivated next step is

to extend this program to a multi-TeV collider, where the same h(→ bb̄) + pmiss
T topology

becomes sensitive to DM and mediator masses an order of magnitude beyond the current



114

limits, and where the thermal WIMP mass range can be directly tested. The muon collider

experiment would constitute a key component of a comprehensive multi-front program

capable of either discovering dark matter or definitively ruling out large classes of WIMP

models in the multi-TeV mass range.



115

Study of Beam-Induced

Background at a Muon Collider

The history of experimental particle physics tells us that colliders have been at the forefront

of scientific discoveries. Each leap in center-of-mass energy has opened a new window into

the structure of matter, from the discovery of the W and Z bosons at the SppS to the

Higgs boson at the LHC. The question facing the field today is: what comes next?

A muon collider has re-emerged as one of the most compelling future colliders. The

core appeal is straightforward: muons are fundamental particles, and so, like electrons,

the collision does not involve the partonic substructure like in proton-proton interactions.

However, muons are approximately 200 times heavier than electrons, which dramatically

suppresses the synchrotron radiation that makes accelerating electrons to multi-TeV en-

ergies very expensive in a circular ring. A muon collider offers a clean, and well-defined

initial state of a lepton collider at energies that would require a proton machine of truly

enormous scale to match [130, 131, 132, 133].

The physics case becomes especially striking at 10 TeV center-of-mass energy. At this

energy, the muon collider benefits from the emission of electroweak gauge bosons from the

incoming muons, and thus effectively acts as a high-luminosity vector boson collider. This

so called Vector Boson Fusion (VBF) regime gives access to processes that would otherwise

Several future collider proposals are currently under active study, and it is useful to

this landscape.

A.1 Physics Case

The physics program of a 10 TeV muon collider is exceptionally broad. The combination

of high energy, a clean leptonic initial state, and the VBF enhancement makes it a discov-

ery machine for new heavy states, as well as a precision instrument for Standard Model

measurements.

• Higgs physics would be transformed, with millions of Higgs bosons produced, rare

While the LHC provides only weak constraints, and the HL-LHC achieves a mod-

• Electroweak precisionmeasurements at these energies are sensitive to BSM physics

as a high-energy precision machine, extending the reach of indirect constraints on

new physics well beyond the scales directly accessible.

• Perhaps most importantly, the high energy frontier opens broad sensitivity to BSM

physics. A 10 TeV muon collider significantly extends the discovery reach for new

particles, including strongly interacting states, additional gauge bosons, and ex-

benefiting from the large available center-of-mass energy, and indirectly via precision

measurements that reveal deviations from Standard Model expectations. This dual

capability ensures sensitivity to a wide range of scenarios, including those that are

challenging for hadron colliders due to backgrounds or limited kinematic reach.

Dark matter searches

As discussed in the previous chapter, a muon collider with its high energy offers sensitivity

to dark matter masses in the multi-TeV regime.

The VBF regime further enhances sensitivity to WIMPs, and crucially to Electroweak

to produce at hadron colliders due to their small cross sections. At 10 TeV even near-

degenerate multiplet states can be pair-produced with appreciable rates, and the soft

charged tracks from the mass splitting becomes detectable [135, 136].

The muon collider is also uniquely sensitive to muon-specific dark sectors, scenarios

in which DM couples preferentially to second lepton generation. Such models are poorly

constrained by both e+e− colliders and hadron machines, making the muon collider po-

tentially the only facility for testing them [137].

A.2 Machine Design

Realizing a muon collider at 3 or 10 TeV requires solving a chain of accelerator physics

challenges that have no direct precedent. The difficulty stems from the muon’s short

lifetime, where a muon at rest decays in approximately 2.2 µs, which means the entire

production, cooling, and acceleration sequence must be completed within a time window

that, even after accounting for relativistic time dilation, is severely constrained. The



119

conceptual layout of the accelerator complex reflects this urgency at every stage.

Figure A.3 shows a schematic layout of the muon collider complex, consisting of five

main subsystems arranged sequentially. In the proton driver, an high-intensity proton

beam, operating at multi-MW beam power, is accelerated and directed onto a target,

producing pions that subsequently decay into muons. The resulting secondary particles

are captured in the front end, where a system of solenoids and RF structures collects

and forms the muon beam. Due to the large initial phase-space volume, the beam is

then passed through a dedicated cooling channel, where ionization cooling reduces its

transverse and longitudinal emittance to achieve the luminosity requirements. The cooled

muons are subsequently accelerated to the desired energy through a sequence of linacs

and recirculating accelerators. Finally, the beams are injected into the collider ring, where

counter-propagating muon beams are brought into collision at the interaction points.

In conventional accelerators, emittance is reduced by synchrotron radiation cooling,

the same effect that limits electron colliders at high energy. Muons, however, decay too

quickly for this process to be effective. Instead, the muon collider relies on “ionisation

cooling”, a technique in which the beam passes through an absorbing material (typically

liquid hydrogen), losing momentum in all directions, while radio-frequency (RF) cavi-

ties restore only the longitudinal component. The net effect is a reduction in transverse

emittance. Figure A.4 shows a schematic view. Ionisation cooling was successfully demon-

strated, in principle, by the international Muon Ionization Cooling Experiment (MICE)

at Rutherford Appleton Laboratory. MICE confirmed that passing muon beams through

Following cooling, the muons are rapidly accelerated through a sequence of recirculat-

collider ring [130, 139].

The collider ring itself is compact compared to hadron collider standards. A 10 TeV

A.3 Detector Design

Designing a detector for a muon collider involves navigating a tension that has no ana-

logue at any existing facility. On one hand, the physics goals demand the capabilities

expected of any next-generation collider detector, which involve excellent tracking reso-

lution, high-granularity calorimetry, good muon identification, and efficient triggering on

complex final states. On the other hand, the muon beams produce an intense and highly

specific background environment, called the beam-induced background (BIB), which is

discussed in detail in the next section that shapes almost every detector design choice.

The reference detector concept developed within the IMCC study [130, 140], is broadly

modeled on the detector concepts developed for future lepton colliders such as ILC and

CLIC, adapted to address the BIB environment. It is organized in the familiar onion-layer

structure, as shown in Figure A.5.

The inner tracker sits closest to the IP and is responsible for reconstructing the

trajectories of charged particles and identifying the primary interaction vertex. It uses

silicon pixel and strip detectors arranged in cylindrical barrel layers and endcap disks.



122

The tracker design must balance the need for low material budget.

The electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) surrounds the tracker and is designed

to measure the energy of photons and electrons with high precision. The reference design

adopts a sampling calorimeter technology based on tungsten absorbers and silicon pad

sensors, closely following the design developed for the CMS High-Granularity Calorimeter

(HGCAL) for the HL-LHC. The high granularity, both longitudinal and transverse, is

essential for two reasons: it enables precise shower reconstruction in a dense collision

environment, and it provides timing information that can be used to discriminate BIB

hits from genuine collision products. This timing capability is central to the calorimeter

mitigation strategy discussed later, including the work described in Section ??.

The hadronic calorimeter (HCAL) extends the calorimeter system to measure hadronic

showers. It uses a similar sampling philosophy with steel absorbers.

The muon system forms the outermost layer, exploiting the fact that muons are

the only charged particles that typically traverse the full calorimeter depth without being

absorbed. At a muon collider, however, the muon system must be carefully designed to

distinguish collision produced muon from the large flux of low-energy muons arriving as

part of the BIB.

A distinctive and critical feature of the detector design is the tungsten nozzle, a pair

of conical shielding absorbers that line the beam pipe in the forward region, extending

from the IP outward at small angles. Their purpose is to intercept the bulk of the BIB

before it reaches the sensitive detector elements. The nozzle geometry is one of the most

actively studied aspects of the detector design, as its shape and material composition have

a direct impact on the residual BIB that the detector systems must handle [141].

A.4 Beam Induced Background

The dominant source of background at a muon collider is different from that encountered at

existing collider experiments, and understanding it is essential to appreciating the detector

design choices.



123

As muons circulate in the collider ring, they decay continuously (µ → e νe νµ). At

the design intensity, O(108) muon decays occur per meter of beam pipe per second in

the vicinity of the IP. The decay products, high energy electrons, positrons and photons

interact with the beam pipe material and the machine lattice. These interactions initiate

electromagnetic cascades, wherein the electrons radiate photons via bremsstrahlung, and

the photons pair produce electron and positron, and so on. The result is a continuous,

diffuse halo of particles: electrons, positrons, photons, neutrons, and charged hadrons,

that flood the detector volume from all angles, largely uncorrelated with the hard collision

at the IP. This is the Beam-Induced Background (BIB) [140].

The most powerful handle available to discriminate BIB from genuine collision products

is timing. Particles produced in the hard scatter at the interaction point travel outward at

approximately the speed of light, arriving at a given detector layer at a time that is well-

predicted by their path length from the origin. BIB particles, by contrast, arrive at the

detector having followed longer, more tortuous paths, scattered off beam pipe elements,

propagating as secondaries and tertiaries through material, and therefore tend to arrive

earlier and later compared to the prompt collision window. The timing distribution of BIB

hits is broad, with a characteristic spread of several nanoseconds, while prompt collision

products are concentrated within a window of roughly ±1 ns around the expected arrival

time [140]. Figure A.6 shows the time of arrival for dominant BIB particle types (neutrons,

photons, and electrons/positrons) with a substantial spread with respect to the bunch

crossing.

This separation in time forms the basis of the primary mitigation strategy. By equip-

ping detector elements with sufficient timing resolution and applying a time-of-flight (ToF)

requirement, by retaining only hits whose arrival time is consistent with a particle origi-

nating from the interaction point, a large fraction of BIB hits can be rejected before any

higher-level reconstruction is done. The silicon sensors in the tracker can achieve resolu-

tions of order 30–100 ps, while calorimeter cells, depending on technology and occupancy,

typically achieve resolutions in the range of a few hundred ps to 1 ns [140].



124

Timing cuts alone do not eliminate BIB entirely. The residual BIB remains substan-

tial, particularly in the calorimeters, and must be addressed by further strategies at the

A.5 Jet reconstruction

Jet reconstruction uses information from almost all subdetector systems with a significant

impact of BIB in all of them, which makes it a difficult task at a muon collider environment.

There exists a preliminary jet reconstruction algorithm which has decent performance but

has room for further improvements. One of the inputs to the reconstruction algorithm are

the calorimeter hits that pass an energy threshold and are within a hit time window of

±0.25 ns of the bunch crossing time.

In order to reduce the hits from BIB, various thresholds were tested by the IMCC

group, and found that a threshold of 2 MeV applied to both ECAL and HCAL was a good

compromise between the jet performance and computing time. It was also found that the

computing time of the jet algorithm grows exponentially with the number of calorimeter

hits, which restricts lowering the threshold below 2 MeV.

dependent pattern stands in clear contrast to the structured shower topology of signal

hits, and underscores the challenge BIB poses to jet reconstruction when these deposits

accumulate into spurious clusters.

Figure A.15 shows the fraction of total ECAL Barrel energy deposited in each layer,

separately for signal and BIB. The BIB energy fraction is heavily skewed toward the first

layer, with approximately 50% of all BIB energy deposited there, falling off rapidly in

subsequent layers. Signal energy, by contrast, follows a more gradual longitudinal profile

consistent with shower development extending through many layers. This sharp front-

loading of BIB energy in the initial layer provides a strong quantitative motivation for

applying a tighter energy threshold specifically to layer 1. Even a modest increase in the

digitization threshold for this layer would reject a substantial fraction of BIB energy with

minimal impact on the signal shower energy, which is spread across many layers.

Figure A.16 (left) shows the time-of-flight distributions of simulated BIB hits in various

ECAL Barrel layers. A trend is observed, where the timing peak shifts to progressively

larger values as the layer number increases, reflecting the additional path length traversed

Figure A.16 (right) shows the distribution of the longitudinal coordinate Z of simu-

lated BIB hits for various ECAL Barrel layers. In the initial layers, BIB hit occupancy

is highest in the central region of the barrel (|Z| ≈ 0), reflecting the dominance of BIB

particles arriving along trajectories close to the beam axis. As the layer number increases,

the Z distribution flattens and becomes more uniform across the barrel length. This

layer- and Z-dependent occupancy pattern suggests a further refinement of the thresh-

old strategy: tighter energy thresholds could be applied not only to the initial layers but

specifically to the central Z region within those layers, where BIB contamination is most

severe. Combined with the layer-dependent timing parametrization motivated by left fig-

ure, this points toward a multidimensional threshold scheme in which the energy threshold

is parametrized jointly in layer number and longitudinal position.

The studies presented here represent a preliminary investigation into BIB mitigation

strategies at the ECAL Barrel digitization stage, motivated by the distinctive spatial,

longitudinal, and timing characteristics of BIB hits compared to signal. The key obser-

vations, that BIB deposits roughly half its energy in the first calorimeter layer, that its



133

hit occupancy is most severe in the central Z region of the initial layers, and that its

time-of-flight distribution shifts systematically with layer depth, collectively point toward

a multidimensional threshold scheme as a promising direction for improvement over the

current uniform 2 MeV baseline.

The modified threshold tested here, applying 5 MeV to the first ECAL Barrel layer

while retaining 2 MeV elsewhere, is intentionally simple and serves as a proof of concept

rather than an optimized solution. It demonstrates that selective tightening of the dig-

itization threshold in BIB-dominated regions can reduce hit occupancy without broadly

impacting the deeper layers where signal shower energy is concentrated. However, the full

parameter space remains largely unexplored. A natural extension would be to parametrize

energy threshold jointly as a function of layer number and longitudinal position Z, target-

ing the central Z, initial-layer region identified as the most BIB-contaminated. Similarly,

a layer-dependent timing window, with the acceptance window center shifted according to

the expected BIB time-of-flight offset in each layer, could provide complementary rejection

power beyond what energy thresholds alone can achieve.

Further improvements could also be pursued at the algorithmic level. The substructure

variables explored in the jet reconstruction studies — including ∆R and ∆Z between

daughter particles offer handles for rejecting fake jets that survive the digitization-level

cuts, and a combined strategy leveraging both digitization thresholds and reconstruction-

level selections may ultimately prove more powerful than either approach in isolation.

Machine learning based approaches, trained on the full set of calorimeter hit features

including position, energy, and timing, could also provide a more flexible and data-driven

path to BIB rejection, and represent an interesting avenue for future study.

It should be noted that the simulations used throughout these studies reflect the current

state of the IMCC detector model and BIB samples, both of which are expected to evolve

as the muon collider feasibility program matures. The BIB environment is sensitive to

the machine optics, shielding geometry, and beam parameters, and future iterations of

the simulation may quantitatively shift the optimal threshold values identified here. The



134

results should therefore be interpreted as directional rather than definitive, and revisited

as more realistic detector and machine models become available.

Taken together, these contributions demonstrate that the digitization stage offers a

tractable and computationally inexpensive handle for BIB mitigation, and that geometry-

and timing-aware threshold schemes merit further systematic study within the IMCC de-

tector optimization effort. The H → bb̄ mass resolution serves as a sensitive and physically

motivated benchmark for this optimization, and future studies should evaluate the impact

of refined threshold strategies on both the jet energy resolution and the fake jet rate in a

consistent framework.

abstracts.value: This is a short review of the current status of the Standard Model calculation of the Muon <math display="inline" id="d1e2848" altimg="si1.svg"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, based on the recently published White Paper. After a brief summary of the theoretically very well determined QED and electroweak contributions, the review focuses on the two main hadronic contributions, the vacuum polarization (HVP) and the light-by-light (HLbL), both for what concerns the lattice as well as the dispersive, data-driven determinations. In view of discrepancies in the data sets used for the dispersive determination of the HVP, the final theoretical value of the Muon <math display="inline" id="d1e2858" altimg="si1.svg"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> in the SM is based on the lattice value for the HVP contribution and an average of the lattice and dispersive determinations for the HLbL contribution. The review ends with a brief outlook on how to address two urgent challenges: (i) reduce the theory uncertainty by a factor four to match the experimental one; (ii) resolve the current puzzles affecting data-driven determinations of the HVP contribution.

abstracts.value: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

titles.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes

abstracts.value: Determining whether every trajectory of the linear system $\dot{x}=Ax$ converges to zero (or, equivalently, whether $A$ is Hurwitz stable) is a fundamental problem in control theory. It arises, for example, in verifying the stability of feedback controllers and state observers, as well as of linearized dynamical models. We study the quantum query complexity of deciding whether a matrix $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ is Hurwitz stable, given an exact normalized block-encoding of $A$. The query complexity is characterized in terms of the system dimension $n$ and a supplied lower bound $0<ν\leq ω_A$ on the imaginary-axis distance $ω_A:=\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}σ_{\min}(A-\mathrm{i}tI)$, where $σ_{\min}(A)$ is the smallest singular value of $A$. We prove a query-complexity lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{n}/ν)$, which holds even when $A$ is restricted to be real and diagonal. For general matrices with nonzero $ω_A$, we encode an approximation of the right-half-plane spectral projector $\operatorname{sign}^+(A):=(I+\operatorname{sign}(A))/2$ as a block of a matrix inverse, where $A$ is Hurwitz if and only if the projector is zero. To test this, we produce a quantum algorithm which determines if a $(β,b,1/(4\sqrt{n}))$-block-encoded projector matrix (like $\operatorname{sign}^+(A)$) is zero or not; for constant success probability, it has complexity $Θ(β\sqrt{n})$. When the zero test is applied to specific approximations of $\operatorname{sign}^+(A)$, this yields an upper bound of $O(\sqrt{n}ν^{-2}\log(\sqrt{n}/ν))$ queries in the general case, and $O(\sqrt{n}ν^{-1}\log n)$ when $A$ is Hermitian or normal. The latter upper bound matches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Thus the dimension dependence of quantum Hurwitz testing is nearly optimal, while the remaining factor in the non-normal case isolates an open conditioning gap.

titles.title: Quantum query complexity of Hurwitz stability testing

abstracts.value: Let $L_n$ be the finite-dimensional irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-module of highest weight $n$. We study the space of highest-weight vectors in $L_n\otimes L_m$ for the diagonal $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-action. The extremal projector constructs these singular vectors and gives operators connecting the highest-weight lines in the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition. We interpret these operators in the Mickelsson-Zhelobenko algebra of the diagonal pair $(\mathfrak{sl}_2\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2, \mathfrak{sl}_2^{\mathrm{diag}})$. A rescaling of their quadratic relation yields the cubic Smith relation $[E,F]=2(H^3-cH)$. This cubic algebra is also known as a Higgs algebra in the physics literature. We express both the central parameter $c$ and the Smith Casimir in terms of the quadratic $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Casimir elements of the two tensor factors. The singular subspace becomes an irreducible Smith module of dimension $\min\{n,m\}+1$, with explicit formulas for the actions of the raising and lowering operators $E$ and $F$. Finally, comparison with finite-dimensional simple Smith modules gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a module to arise from this tensor-product construction.

titles.title: Smith Algebra from $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Tensor Product Branching via the Mickelsson-Zhelobenko Algebra

abstracts.value: Subregions in gauge theories give rise to edge modes and corner charges supported on their boundaries. While this is well-established classically and in quantum lattice gauge theories, the fate of corner modes remains poorly understood in continuum quantum field theories owing to their distributional nature. In this paper, we revisit this challenge and propose a new corner operator for a regional Cauchy slice algebra generated by local gauge-invariant observables of scalar QED in Minkowski spacetime. The corner mode is given by the longitudinal electric field sourced by the matter outside the subregion and thus constitutes a centre for the regional algebra. Our main goal is to show that there exists a perturbative GNS state on this algebra that quantises this mode. Pulling back the Fock vacuum to the slice, we construct this state by renormalising the divergences arising from the lack of temporal smearing. We clarify that the inclusion of the new centre mode necessitates a further renormalisation on the corner of the region, thereby physically distinguishing it and breaking the translation invariance of the state. Our work shows how the requirements of locality, renormalisability, and positivity together put strong constraints on the existence of a continuum quantum field theory which supports corner modes as genuine quantum operators. We finish with comments about the von Neumann completion of the regional algebra, as well as possible physical interpretations of the renormalised vacuum state.

titles.title: Longitudinal electric corner modes in continuum quantum gauge theory with matter

abstracts.value: We consider the RP$^2$ model on the two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. It is obtained by replacing the spin in the standard classical Heisenberg model with a director, which does not distinguish two opposite directions. Unlike the standard classical Heisenberg model or the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, the RP$^2$ (and its cousin RP$^3$) model allows point vortex defects classified by $π_1(RP^2)= Z_2$ in two dimensions. It is tempting to expect the $Z_2$ vortices to induce a phase transition analogous to the well-established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(2) model (XY model) in two dimensions. Indeed, the possibilities of a critical phase or a critical point with power-law correlations of the order parameter in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models have been discussed in the literature. However, the challenging nature of the problem has prevented a definitive conclusion on the phase diagram so far. In this paper, we report a rigorous mathematical proof by Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 6 Astra) that the absolute value of the two-point correlation function of order parameters at distance $r$ in the RP$^2$ and RP$^3$ models on the two-dimensional square lattice is bounded above by $C_β\exp{(-c_β[\log(2+r)]^2)}$ for any finite inverse temperature $β\ge0$, with positive constants $C_β$ and $c_β$ depending only on $β$. Namely, the correlation function decays faster than any power of $r$. The proof is formalized and verified in Lean; the formalization is publicly available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23548847 . A heuristic argument based on a one-parameter effective theory ansatz at large distances combined with the rigorous correlation bound suggests (but does not prove) that the $Z_2$ vortices are always unbound at any nonzero temperature.

titles.title: Faster-than-power-law decay of order parameter correlations in the two-dimensional RP$^2$ model: a rigorous result by vibe-proving

abstracts.value: We propose a phenomenological framework toward a Three-Body Holonomy Standard Model in which the number three is selected by the minimal primitive cyclic structure of a democratic many-body interaction network. The resulting threefold holonomy information is assumed to survive in $(3+1)$ dimensions as an internal three-state space. A Lorentz-invariant six-fermion interaction provides a candidate microscopic origin of the internal cyclic correlations, with their matching to Wilson holonomy left as a dynamical requirement. The parity-related holonomy sectors of the underlying $(1+1)$-dimensional Dirac system motivate left- and right-handed internal structures and a trinification-like $SU(3)_C\times SU(3)_L\times SU(3)_R$ gauge completion. Vertical holonomy selects a $2+1$ splitting, while spontaneous left-right vacuum misalignment provides a possible route to chiral symmetry breaking. Horizontal holonomy organizes the three-family mass structure, with heavy-fermion mixing generating effective flavor and CP-violating patterns. Although a complete ultraviolet derivation remains open, the framework provides a unified scenario connecting primitive three-body dynamics to gauge symmetry, symmetry breaking, and fermion flavor.

titles.title: Toward a Three-Body Holonomy Standard Model

abstracts.value: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

titles.title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer

abstracts.value: Quantum processors are now used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data. A circuit encodes each record, the device returns expectation values, and a classical model learns from them. A recent report claimed large gains from such features, gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. These claims are hard to check, because a quantum device is not a static function. Its state changes from job to job and from one calibration to the next, and that drift can leak information about the outcome into the features. We propose a five-step protocol for testing claims of this kind. It runs a circuit that carries no data in the same jobs as the real one. It checks whether the hardware leaves a recognizable mark on each job. It compares random and natural assignments of records to jobs, replays the null results under other submission orders, and closes the leak with a job-purged backtest. We apply it, pre-registered, to the HSBC and IBM study of fill probabilities in bond trading, which reported a large hardware-only gain. We use a public analog task and run the study's circuit on a 129-qubit chain of an IBM Heron processor. Under controlled assignment the hardware features give no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces the ideal features about as well as shot noise allows. Yet every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A circuit with no data at all predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that overlap removes the effect. The protocol costs under an hour of processor time and is designed for any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.

titles.title: Testing hardware quantum machine learning claims with a null circuit: fill prediction on Binance futures with 129 qubits of an IBM Heron processor

abstracts.value: Postselection can enhance the performance of a selected quantum battery branch, raising the question of whether the optimum can always be achieved by product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems. For battery auxiliary states obtained by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy reduces to a generalized Rayleigh quotient. For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum if and only if the eigenspace associated with the largest generalized eigenvalue contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap therefore occurs precisely when this eigenspace is one dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector. Noisy W and GHZ states display qualitatively different behavior: the three qubit W state exhibits a strict gap throughout 0<p<1, whereas the three qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as the coupling strength is varied. By contrast, the outcome averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, showing that the joint measurement advantage is genuinely postselective.

titles.title: Entangled Measurement Outcomes for Optimal Postselection in Quantum Batteries

abstracts.value: Ground-based millimeter and submillimeter telescopes produce astronomical maps that contain a combination of noise inherent to themselves as well as contamination from foregrounds, with the strongest foreground being fluctuating atmospheric emission. While the emission of the turbulent atmosphere itself follows a scale-free power law, the atmosphere as seen by the telescope is modified by the properties of the instrument optics. A naive power-law extrapolation of the atmospheric noise spectrum ignores the blurring effect of the near-field beam, which becomes more pronounced for larger telescope apertures and at higher multipoles. In this work, we use a toy model to derive a semianalytic estimate of the atmospheric noise spectrum that takes into account the effects of near-field optics. We show that it has an appreciable effect for large-aperture telescopes, suggesting that ultra-sensitive, high-resolution experiments are not necessarily limited by the atmosphere on small angular scales. We also present an estimate of the atmospheric knee as a function of the primary aperture, the atmospheric scale height, and the outer scale of turbulence.

titles.title: The Effect of Large Apertures on Atmospheric Noise Spectra for Millimeter-wave Telescopes

abstracts.value: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally challenging, often requiring effective reversal of many-body dynamics. Here, we propose an alternative approach to probing operator spreading through local quantum fluctuations, using only forward evolution and local measurements. Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, we introduce a differential local variance and establish a rigorous bound connecting it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, we derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. In integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs reveal qualitatively consistent propagation fronts. Our results establish local quantum fluctuations as an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading.

titles.title: Probing Operator Spreading with Local Quantum Fluctuations

abstracts.value: Quantum geometry is conventionally understood in parameter or momentum space and need not be related to a geometry in configuration space. Here we show for Dirac fermions in a background electromagnetic field that an induced Lorentzian geometry is generated from the fermionic quantum metric. We study a Lorentz covariant phase space worldline path integral construction, whose application of the adiabatic theorem onto spin degrees of freedom leads to the appearance of the Berry phase at $O(\hbar)$, and the quantum metric at $O(\hbar^2)$ in the worldline action. Both the Feynman and retarded/advanced propagators are examined in 3+1 and 2+1 dimensions, whose different on-shell implementations lead to related quantum metrics; QED/QED${}_3$ and condensed matter Dirac theory are considered. An effective theory is found by integrating out the momenta degrees of freedom, which gives rise to an emergent Lorentzian metric in configuration space, whose perturbation to the flat metric is dependent on the quantum metric and the background field strength. Apart from the spin degrees of freedom encoded into the Berry phase, the effective theory describes a scalar particle moving in the induced quantum geometry. Phenomenological applications to the covariant geometry are further studied using spectral holonomy in a gapped 3-dimensional Dirac material.

titles.title: Induced Lorentzian geometry from the fermionic quantum metric

abstracts.value: Ekholm and Shende's skeins-on-branes formalism provides invariant counts of holomorphic curves with boundary on a Maslov zero Lagrangian within a Calabi-Yau 3-fold. This paper proves the orientation relations required for worldsheet skein relations to cancel codimension-one boundary strata. However, standard Cauchy-Riemann Fredholm orientations reveal an unexpected sign puzzle: the orientation relation at a curve with a hyperbolic boundary crossing depends on whether the crossing lies on distinct boundary components or the same component. This domain-dependent sign contradicts the uniform crossing relations of the HOMFLYPT skein algebra. We show that this discrepancy is resolved by passing to an anti-holomorphic orientation convention. We establish all required orientation comparisons in the general setting of an oriented Lagrangian submanifold of a 6-dimensional symplectic manifold.

titles.title: Orientations for skein-valued curve counting

abstracts.value: We present MAGIKS, a multimodal framework for gravitational-wave (GW)-triggered kilonova identification that formulates counterpart search as query-conditioned gallery retrieval. Following an align-before-fuse design, MAGIKS combines GW source parameters and sky-localization maps with irregularly sampled multiband optical light curves and sky coordinates. A time-aware supervised contrastive objective provides coarse cross-modal alignment, while dual cross-attention evaluates consistency between optical coordinates and GW localization, and between GW parameters and optical evolution. We train and evaluate MAGIKS on simulated binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole mergers, Rubin Observatory kilonova light curves from regular survey observations and target-of-opportunity follow-up, GW-detected mergers without Rubin-detectable kilonova counterparts, and realistic non-kilonova contaminants. In independent galleries with one true counterpart and time- and sky-compatible distractors, MAGIKS outperforms optical-only and sky-localization-only ranking, with increasing gains as galleries grow. At 5000 candidates, it ranks the counterpart first for 39.8% of queries, versus 4.8% and 0.2% for these baselines. In a GW170817 study, we generate counterfactual Rubin observations using released GW parameters and three-dimensional localization, the measured counterpart position, and host distance. At the same gallery size, MAGIKS achieves top-1 and top-10 retrieval rates of 87.3% and 95.7%. It correctly classifies 94.2% of associated and non-associated GW-optical pairs. In a separate crossed-pair experiment, its matching score responds significantly to controlled changes in all five tested GW parameters. These results support GW-conditioned kilonova candidate prioritisation for future multi-messenger follow-up.

titles.title: MAGIKS: Multimodal Alignment and Gravitational-Wave-Conditioned Interaction for Kilonova Search

abstracts.value: Gravitational waves from eccentric compact binary coalescences trace dynamical binary formation, but matched-filtering searches responsible for most detections rely on quasicircular templates. Quantifying any sensitivity loss is crucial for assessing population completeness and the need for dedicated eccentric template banks. We present the first systematic GstLAL search study spanning eccentricities up to $e_{\rm 15Hz}=0.99$ and broad ranges of chirp mass, mass ratio, inclination, and aligned spin. Using TEOBResumS-Dalí waveforms, we inject eccentric signals and measure recovered signal-to-noise ratio, signal-consistency statistics, false-alarm rate, and sensitive volume and distance. For high-mass binaries ($\mathcal{M}_c\gtrsim30\,M_\odot$), sensitive distance is nearly independent of eccentricity, demonstrating that greater eccentricity does not necessarily reduce search sensitivity. In contrast, for low-mass binaries, sensitive distance falls by up to $\sim50\%$ near $e_{\rm 15Hz}\approx0.75$. Although the absolute loss in reach is modest given their low quasicircular sensitivity, this relative reduction exceeds the increase in sensitive distance between the second and third observing runs of the LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA collaboration and is consistent with previous low-mass studies. We also find that waveform matches at fixed source parameters substantially overpredict search sensitivity loss, meaning that the pipeline's signal-consistency test and maximization over its template bank mitigate much of the predicted sensitivity loss. This highlights the need for end-to-end injection campaigns to establish the detectability of eccentric binaries.

titles.title: More Eccentric, Not Always Less Detectable: High Mass Holds Its Ground, Low Mass Loses Reach

abstracts.value: We study the light nucleus production in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $13$~TeV reported by the ALICE Collaboration within the color string fragmentation framework. We adopt the Schwinger mechanism with string tension fluctuations as the particle production mechanism describing the $p_T$ spectrum. The approximately thermal behavior observed in the light-nucleus spectra motivates the use of a perturbative series expansion of the $q$-Gaussian string tension fluctuations around $q=1$. The resulting $p_T$ spectrum is expressed as a perturbative series expansion around the thermal distribution with nonthermal corrections given by Gamma distributions, providing closed forms for the effective temperature, moments, and cumulants. In the superstatistical framework, the associated temperature fluctuations show that the medium in which light nuclei are produced is out of equilibrium. Additionally, we derive closed formulas for the coalescence parameter at arbitrary order, which agree well with experimental data. Our results also show that the mass--temperature relation ($T_N/m_N \approx AT_A/m_A$) between the nucleons and nuclei is not preserved in the coalescence process.

titles.title: Nonthermal coalescence parameter of light nuclei production in pp collisions at LHC energies

abstracts.value: The neutron star (NS) mass distribution serves as a crucial probe of the dense matter equation of state (EOS) and core-collapse supernova explosion mechanisms. Although observations reveal a bimodal NS mass distribution, existing theoretical simulations often struggle to naturally reproduce the high-mass peak, and the impact of the quark-hadron phase transition (PT) in high-density nuclear matter remains largely unexplored. Employing the 1D general-relativistic hydrodynamics code GR1D with hybrid EOSs incorporating a first-order PT (RDF1.1 and RDF1.2), we systematically simulate core-collapse supernovae for progenitors with zero-age main-sequence masses ranging from 13 to 120 $M_\odot$. Our results reveal a threefold impact of the PT onset density on the final supernova fate: in low-compactness progenitors, an early PT truncates accretion and produces less massive NSs; in the critical-compactness regime, it facilitates successful explosions; and in high-compactness progenitors, it accelerates black hole formation. Compared with the $\sim 1.4\,M_\odot$ peak typical of the conventional core-collapse scenario, the inclusion of the PT produces NSs with masses centered around $1.70\,M_\odot$ for RDF1.1 and within $1.55$--$1.70\,M_\odot$ for RDF1.2. Furthermore, we identify a novel formation channel whereby low-compactness progenitors with failed initial shocks can form more massive NSs via a PT-induced second shock. Due to the fixed nature of the PT boundary, the final NS masses exhibit a pronounced clustering effect. This study elucidates the critical role of the quark-hadron PT in shaping the NS mass distribution, providing important astrophysical constraints on the properties of high-density nuclear matter and the formation mechanism of massive NSs.

titles.title: Effect of quark-hadron phase transitions on the neutron star mass distribution

abstracts.value: We show that reversible in-place quantum addition modulo $2^n-1$ can be implemented in constant Toffoli depth using $O(n)$ space, provided that the variables are encoded in a certain non-standard form. Using measurement-based uncomputation, the Toffoli depth can be reduced to one. We also present space-depth tradeoffs and an application to programmable rotations.

titles.title: Encoded reversible addition in constant Toffoli depth

abstracts.value: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing a meson parton distribution function (PDF) or parton distribution amplitude (PDA) at a fixed scale from a finite set of Mellin moments. At finite moment order this map is ill posed in the Hadamard sense: the moments do not determine a unique, stable pointwise $x$-dependence, and small data perturbations can produce large changes in the reconstruction. We regularize the problem by restricting the admissible function class through constraints justified by first principles---support on $x\in[0,1]$, endpoint vanishing, unit normalization, and, for the pion, the exact $x\leftrightarrow 1-x$ symmetry---and by complementing these hard constraints with differentiable penalties that suppress the spurious multiple maxima and central concavity changes typical of ill-posed inversions. We parameterize the unknown function with two interchangeable neural cores, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN), and find that the KAN reconstructs the target distributions more accurately, most markedly in the asymmetric (kaon) case. We attribute this advantage to the locality of the B-spline basis underlying the KAN, which localizes corrections during moment matching and damps the global oscillations to which the MLP is prone. Benchmarks against synthetic targets, using both ten and five input moments, support these conclusions.

titles.title: Reconstructing Meson Parton Distributions from Mellin Moments with Artificial Neural Networks

abstracts.value: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

titles.title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity

abstracts.value: We study linearized gravitational reconstruction in global AdS$_4$ with dynamical scalar matter, building on vacuum Einstein perturbations with fixed boundary metric and nontrivial normalizable data. External scalar sources prepare an excited state and modify the holographic Ward identities, while subsequent evolution can proceed without boundary driving. Separating the bulk matter-sourced response from vacuum perturbations, we derive an electric quadrupole master equation with the matter-dependent corrections required by the Einstein constraints. We also verify that a cylindrical boundary integral reproduces the Regge--Wheeler master field mode by mode, without identifying it with the full global Fefferman--Graham reconstruction. For weakly interacting scalars that become massless in the flat-space limit, we extract the Bondi shear and news from retarded gravitational evolution. The resulting supertranslation memory agrees numerically with the outgoing energy redistribution and the quadrupole moment of the boundary work. In the ordered flat-space limit, later boundary controls leave the first event's waveform unchanged, despite cancelling residual gravitational modes at finite AdS radius.

titles.title: Gravitational Memory from AdS States in the Flat-Space Limit

abstracts.value: Local star-forming regions have recently been the subject of scrutiny as cosmic-ray accelerators and sources of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emissions. The Cygnus-X region is one of the richest star forming regions in the galaxy and over the last few decades has been extensively studied. Here we report the detection of a star-forming region located in the southern part of Cygnus-X, Sharpless 106 (S106), using the HAWC Observatory. The S106 region is spatially located near the cataloged gamma-ray source 1LHAASO J2027+3657. In this work, we perform a multi-wavelength analysis of S106, by combining HAWC data with re-analysis of Fermi-LAT and archival Chandra data. We construct a fully leptonic model for the multi-wavelength emission from S106 from a single population of high-energy leptons, with the gamma-rays greater than 1 TeV being produced by inverse Compton scattering of the locally-produced IR photon field from S106 itself. Our models show that hadronic mechanisms are not always required to explain the observed flux from gamma-ray star-forming regions and that understanding the specific details of local photon fields is crucial to modeling the multi-wavelength emission from star-forming regions.

titles.title: HAWC, Fermi-LAT and Chandra Detections of High Energy Particles in the S106 Star Forming Region

abstracts.value: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $Λ$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.

titles.title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control

abstracts.value: We present the phase diagram of a one-dimensional quantum Rabi zigzag chain under an artificial gauge field, which is implemented via phase-modulated next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) hopping. For a system size of $N=8$, we analytically determine the order parameters and critical thresholds, identifying five distinct superradiant phases. For strong nearest-neighbor (NN) coupling, the system exhibits either a ferro-superradiant (FSR) or an antiferro-superradiant (AFSR) phase depending on its sign. Increasing NNN coupling induces a stripe antiferro-superradiant (sAFSR) phase with antiparallel NNN and parallel NN displacements, which is distinct from the conventional AFSR phase. Tuning the magnetic flux drives the system into chiral or antichiral superradiant phases with opposite ground-state photon currents, which are different from the conventional superradiant phases. Remarkably, geometric frustration within each triangular plaquette stabilizes chiral phases even at small magnetic flux while suppressing the sAFSR phase, which vanishes for $N=6$. Mapping the system onto an effective magnetic Hamiltonian yields an analogous phase diagram featuring distinct magnetic phases, offering insight into the anomalous superradiant phases. This equivalence establishes a quantum optical platform for simulating chiral magnetism.

titles.title: Anomalous superradiant phases in a quantum Rabi zigzag chain under a synthetic gauge field

abstracts.value: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $θ_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

titles.title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon

abstracts.value: A recently constructed superstring field theory has two decoupled sectors, the physical superstring and a shadow sector with a second copy of the superstring. These are both expanded around the same background conformal field theory and the theory is independent of marginal deformations of this common background. A form of the action is presented that is symmetric between the two sectors. A generalisation of this theory is given in which the two sectors can be expanded around two different backgrounds, and the theory is independent under separate marginal deformations of the two background conformal field theories.

titles.title: Superstring Field Theory with Double Background Independence

abstracts.value: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.

titles.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory

abstracts.value: This paper investigates a quantum relay-assisted free-space optical (FSO) communication system in which a decode-and-forward relay is powered by time-switching optical energy harvesting and forwards the decoded information using displaced squeezed signaling (DSS). To obtain a physically con sistent description of turbulence-induced loss for non-classical signaling, each hop is modeled as a pure-loss bosonic chan nel whose random transmissivity follows a truncated Gamma Gamma law, i.e., the Gamma-Gamma irradiance conditioned on the physically admissible range of a transmittance. Under this channel, coherent states remain pure, whereas squeezed states are mapped to mixed Gaussian states. Under Helstrom-optimal detection, the average error of the coherent hop is derived in exact Laplace-series form. For the DSS hop, we derive the output states, a closed-form Gaussian fidelity with rigorous two sided bounds on the Helstrom error, and prove the existence of a loss-aware optimal photon partition. Furthermore, we prove that optimized squeezing preserves both the turbulence-induced diversity order and the leading asymptotic constant of coherent relaying, so that its benefit is a finite-photon-budget effect, and that an interior throughput-optimal harvesting fraction exists. A covariance-preserving benchmark with an exact series representation yields an analytical upper bound on the achievable throughput whose absolute gap vanishes as the relay photon budget grows. Numerical results based on the exact mixed-state Helstrom error quantify the benefit of squeezing and the regime in which it is useful.

titles.title: Time-Switching Energy-Harvesting Quantum Relay-Assisted FSO Communication with Displaced Squeezed Signaling

abstracts.value: A score-based diffusion model is trained on the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model, the lattice representation of the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model. Neural networks are trained on three different coarse-grainings of the same training set to implement a multiscale sampling scheme that modestly improves both the accuracy and computational cost of direct sampling on the finest lattice. Stein (or Schwinger-Dyson) diagnostics for the two-point correlation function are introduced to assess the quality of the learned score without relying on reverse diffusion sampling. These diagnostics are also incorporated into an additional training loss. We discuss several technical considerations relevant to implementing diffusion models on $S^2$. These include a consideration of lifting the network input to $S^3$, as in the $CP^1$ representation, and developing a boundary-layer approximation to the short-time spherical heat kernel that extends its usefulness to larger diffusion times.

titles.title: Diffusion models for the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model

abstracts.value: We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first fully automated verification framework for QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation. Our framework exploits the structure of the simulation algorithm: Hamiltonians are given as weighted sums of Pauli strings, embedded into larger unitaries through block encodings, and transformed into time-evolution operators by quantum signal processing (QSP). Using a symbolic Pauli-sum semantics for ancilla-indexed circuit blocks, our verifier proves that the distinguished all-zero ancilla block is proportional to the target Hamiltonian and infers the subnormalization factor automatically. It then verifies the QSP layer by extracting the implemented polynomial transformation and certifying its approximation error. This structure-aware abstraction is essential for scalability. Composing our verified block encoding and QSP wrapper yields an estimated macro-expanded size of about 1.52 million gates. The verifier certifies the block encoding once and checks the QSP layer through its abstract interface, without expanding the oracle calls. Our implementation verifies block encodings of structured Pauli-sum Hamiltonians with up to 256 system qubits and verifies QSP Hamiltonian-simulation instances by extracting their implemented polynomials and checking the resulting approximation bounds. These results show that fully automated verification can handle common Hamiltonian-simulation circuits at substantial scale when it exploits their algorithmic structure.

titles.title: Automated Verification of Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing
